stem: A 70-year-old woman with a 25-year history of treatment with antipsychotic medications for schizophrenia complains of the onset of writhing tongue and finger movements. What is the probable cause?
explanation:
Tardive dyskinesia
Tardive dyskinesia is a movement disorder associated with the long-term use of antipsychotics. It can cause a wide range of involuntary, sudden movements such as lip-smacking, chewing, tongue protrusion, choreiform hand movements and pelvic thrusting. Symptoms can be severe enough to affect normal functioning, and can be exacerbated by stress. In this case, clues to the correct cause lie in the duration of the antipsychotic treatment, the nature of the movement disorder and the age of the patient.

Akathisia
Akathisia is incorrect. Although akathisia is also associated with antipsychotic use and increased movement, a key feature is an inner subjective and unpleasant feeling of restlessness associated with a compulsion to move. It is also associated with recent antipsychotic addition or dose change.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is incorrect. The question asks for the most probable cause. Although HD is typically thought of as a young-onset condition, there have been cases of HD presenting much later in life with choreiform movements; however, this is very rare.

Parkinsonism
Parkinsonism is incorrect. The symptoms in the vignette do not fit - they are described as choreiform in nature. Pseudo-parkinsonism associated with antipsychotic use is associated with tremor, rigidity and bradyphrenia.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Patients with Wilson’s disease present much earlier, and other options in the MCQ are much more probable. Useful further information on the management of antipsychotic induced side effects can be found in the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry. Causes of tardive dyskinesia Tardive dyskinesia occurs in a number of patients who have had long-term treatment with antipsychotic agents. This consists of choreo-athetoid movements that are often first evident in the fingers and tongue, but later become more generalized. Other notes Huntington’s disease and Wilson’s disease present with tremors and chore, but usually have an earlier onset. Parkinsonism is characterised by resting tremor and bradykinesia. Akathisia is characterised by motor restlessness. Parkinson’s symptoms and akathisia can be caused by antipsychotic medications.

stem: A 70-year-old-man arrives at the Emergency Department an hour after he felt light headed and collapsed to the ground. He told the two paramedics who accompanied him that he has double vision whenever he looks to the right. On examination he is conscious and alert. There is ptosis and a dilated pupil on the left and the left eye is deviated downwards. Right eye movements are normal, as are the right pupillary reflexes. The remainder of the cranial nerves appear to be intact. He has a right hemiplegia. Occlusion of which one of the following arteries is most likely to be responsible for the above neurological deficit in this patient?
options: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery
explanation:
Paramedian branches of the basilar artery
This man presents with left third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis. The lesion is thus localised to the midbrain at the level of the third nerve nucleus. This region is supplied by paramedian branches of the basilar artery or by branches of the posterior cerebral artery. This is the neurological syndrome known as Weber syndrome. Weber syndrome may be produced by various aetiologies (tumour, granulomatous disease, vasculitis, etc) but stroke is one of the more common causes.

Anterior cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. An occlusion here is principally associated with contralateral hemiparesis, with the legs weaker than the arms (due to involvement of the medial frontal lobe which topographically represents the legs on the motor homunculus).

Anterior communicating cerebral artery
Anterior communicating cerebral artery is incorrect. The anterior communicating artery connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries and is located close to the optic chiasm. Aneurysms, rather than occlusions, of this vessel are more common and can manifest with visual field defects.

Middle cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery is incorrect. An occlusion here is principally associated with contralateral hemiparesis, with the arm weaker than the leg.

Vertebral artery
Vertebral artery is incorrect. The vertebral artery is potentially correct as occlusion (eg due to dissection) here can be associated with distal embolisation further up the brainstem. However, vertebral artery occlusion more usually occludes the origin of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and presents with the lateral medullary syndrome.

stem: An 85-year-old obese woman comes to the Elderly Medicine Clinic for review, complaining of poor mobility due to bilateral anterior knee pain. She has a past history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3 (CKD 3) and obesity. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, and her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her body mass index is 35 kg/m2. Knee flexion is limited to 30 degrees bilaterally due to pain, and there is significant anterior crepitus. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Topical ibuprofen
This woman is likely to have osteoarthritis as a result of ‘wear and tear’, given her age and history of obesity. The most appropriate initial intervention is therefore simple analgesia. Given it is unsuitable to use systemic non-steroidal agents due to the presence of CKD 3, topical treatments should be considered. It is important to remember to advise on non-pharmacological interventions such as exercise and weight loss. Guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) suggests a review of multiple pharmacological and non-pharmacological management options.

Celecoxib
Celecoxib is incorrect. Selective cyclo-oxygenase 2 inhibitors pose an increased risk of cardiovascular events and gastrointestinal bleeds, and are normally considered only for short-term use. This patient has a number of existing cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, hypertension and CKD. It is important to halve the dose of celecoxib in patients who are also receiving fluconazole.

Dihydrocodeine
Dihydrocodeine is incorrect. Opioids, eg codeine, would normally be added as a second-line therapy due to their higher rate of adverse effects, particularly constipation in patients who are less mobile. Prolonged use of opioids may lead to dependence and addiction. Beware of the possibility of poor opioid excretion in patients with CKD, leading to opioid accumulation and toxicity.

Intra-articular corticosteroids
Intra-articular corticosteroids is incorrect. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are normally reserved for patients with symptoms that are uncontrolled despite medical therapy, as they can result in joint infections and must be performed repeatedly. It is important to counsel the patient that they may experience a transient increase in pain post-injection, for up to 24 hours.

Naproxen
Naproxen is incorrect. While non-steroidal agents would be effective, in a patient with hypertension and CKD 3, non-steroidals pose a risk of acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia and are therefore not recommended. Nonsteroidal agents may be considered in some people who have failed topical non-steroidal agents and paracetamol. However, gastroprotective treatment should also be offered to the patient.

stem: An elderly man is admitted to the ICU and put on intermittent positive-pressure ventilation. Which one of the following statements is true when comparing positive pressure ventilation with spontaneous ventilation?
options: Venous return and cardiac output fall
explanation:
Venous return and cardiac output fall
Answering this question requires an awareness of the cardio-pulmonary circulation. Recall that in the normal situation, inspiration increases venous return and increases cardiac output. When lung pressures are elevated, such as during positive-pressure ventilation, venous return will fall, which will reduce cardiac output. This will reduce blood pressure. Intermittent positive-pressure ventilation Effects of increased lung volume: Lung volumes are increased: during intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (IPPV), lung volumes are significantly increased when compared with spontaneous ventilation Pulmonary vascular resistance is increased: a large tidal volume causes a rise in pulmonary vascular resistance, which may lead to pulmonary hypertension and/or right ventricular compromise The over-inflated alveoli cause compression of the alveolar blood vessels Moreover, the resultant increase in right ventricle volume may impede left ventricle (LV) filling (ventricular interdependence) Hyperinflation also leads to prostaglandin release, which may be a protective mechanism against lung injury. Effects of increased intrathoracic pressure: Intrathoracic pressure is increased: the intrathoracic pressure is increased at all points in the respiratory cycle Inspiration during IPPV increases intrathoracic pressure and so increases right atrial pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, therefore leading to decreased venous return The increased intrathoracic pressure also decreases the gradient across the LV that it has to work against, which results in a decreased afterload. Both these effects reduce intrathoracic blood volume.

Lung volumes are decreased
Lung volumes are decreased is incorrect. As described, lung volumes increase.

Pulmonary vascular resistance is decreased
Pulmonary vascular resistance is decreased is incorrect. As described, pulmonary vascular resistance increases.

Systemic blood pressure rises
Systemic blood pressure rises is incorrect. As described, blood pressure is reduced.

Intrathoracic pressure is decreased
Intrathoracic pressure is decreased is incorrect. As described, intrathoracic pressure increases.

stem: An 84-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency department by her daughter after she found her to be suffering from an offensive vaginal discharge. The woman suffers from severe dementia and moved to a nursing home 1 year earlier. When you review her in the Emergency department she has a mini mental test score of 8. Some time later you discover that swabs are consistent with gonorrhoea infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate action after prescribing antibiotics for her?
options: Informal inquiry at the nursing home
explanation:
Tell the police
The evidence is that this woman has severe dementia; as such it would be almost impossible for her to form a consenting sexual relationship.

Informal inquiry at the nursing home
Informal inquiry at the nursing home is incorrect. The likelihood is that a crime has been committed. As such making an informal inquiry is inappropriate as it may alert the perpetrator of any crime that they have been discovered.

Contact tracing
Contact tracing is incorrect. Given this woman is unable to consent and has severe dementia, it’s unlikely she can give any information as to contacts.

Inform the daughter
Inform the daughter is incorrect. Informing the daughter runs the risk that she may take action herself, preventing proper investigation of any sexual abuse.

Take no further action
Take no further action is incorrect. Taking no further action, in view of the fact that gonorrhoea is sexually transmitted, is not acceptable.

stem: A 72-year-old man is prescribed a glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray for his angina. When he is reviewed in the clinic he is found to be using between five and eight sprays per day, and a decision is made to convert him to a maximal dose of GTN tablets. He returns a few weeks later, however, to complain that his angina has got worse and that he no longer seems to respond to GTN. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for nitrate tolerance?
options: Increase in nitric oxide (NO) synthetase activity
Upregulation of smooth muscle NO receptors
explanation:
Generation of reactive oxygen species
The phenomenon of nitrate tolerance was first described 30+ years ago, but the pharmacological basis has only been elucidated more recently. It is thought that chronic nitrate therapy may increase vascular oxidative stress, which results in enhanced degradation of nitric oxide (NO) and reduced bioavailability. Resulting reactive oxygen and reactive nitrate species then lead to inhibition of the bioactivation of exogenously administered nitrate. Reference: Gutterman, D. D. 2007. Combating nitrate tolerance. Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology, 27, 1673–1676,

Downregulation of haem oxygenase activity
Downregulation of haem oxygenase activity is incorrect. Up-regulation of haem oxygenase-1 (HO-1) activity may be an important means of overcoming nitrate resistance.

Increase in nitric oxide (NO) synthetase activity
Increase in nitric oxide (NO) synthetase activity is incorrect. Nitric oxide synthase is the rate limiting enzyme in nitric oxide formation, which is decreased in the context of oxidative stress.

Primary increase in NO degradation
Increase in NO degradation is incorrect. Although there is degradation of nitric oxide activity, the underlying mechanism is generation of oxidative free radicals, hence generation of reactive oxygen species is the preferred option.

Upregulation of smooth muscle NO receptors
Upregulation of smooth muscle NO receptors is incorrect. Nitric oxide is a freely mobile chemical transmitter that does not have a specific receptor. Angina (Stable).

stem: You are auditing digoxin dose versus previous medical history in the population of patients admitted to the local hospital against local guidelines put in place by a previous registrar in cardiology. A reduced regular dose of 62.5 mcg/day is indicated in the elderly population. What is the primary pharmacokinetic reason for the dose reduction in older adults?
explanation:
Reduced renal clearance
Reduced digoxin clearance via the kidneys is seen in the elderly; dose reduction is therefore required. The elimination half-life of digoxin is about 40 h in patients with normal renal function, but it can be prolonged to 96 h in severe renal impairment.

Decreased intestinal metabolism
Decreased intestinal metabolism is incorrect. Around 10% of digoxin is metabolised within the intestine, and this process may be diminished in older adults. However, the impact of this on digoxin concentrations is much less than the effect of declining renal function.

Decreased GI absorption
Decreased GI absorption is incorrect. Around 70% of digoxin is absorbed after oral administration, and this does not change significantly in older adults.

Increased tissue distribution
Increased tissue distribution is incorrect. Digoxin is distributed widely to body tissues, irrespective of age.

Reduced protein binding
Reduced protein binding is incorrect. Plasma proteins generally only fall significantly in patients with severe underlying liver or kidney disease, or malabsorption, hence reduced protein binding is not the reason for reduced dosing.

stem: A 72-year-old woman who is taking warfarin for long-standing atrial fibrillation develops a chronic cough. This is found to be due to a reactivation of tuberculosis and she is started on appropriate therapy. Unfortunately her INR is found to fall from 2.4 to 1.3. Which one of the following agents is likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Rifampicin
Rifampicin is a cytochrome p450 enzyme inducer; as such it leads to increased me-tabolism of warfarin and a fall in INR. Other examples of enzyme inducers that lead to re-duced INR include: phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John’s Wort. In contrast, drugs capable of inhibiting warfarin metabolism and increasing INR include: erythromycin, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, and allopurinol.

Chloramphenicol
Chloramphenicol is incorrect. Chloramphenicol may enhance the effect of warfarin, possibly through a proteinbinding interaction and displacement of warfarin. INR requires careful monitoring.

Ethambutol
Ethambutol is incorrect. Ethambutol is less likely to interact with warfarin than other anti-tuberculous medications.

Isoniazid
Isoniazid is incorrect. Co-administration of isoniazid may increase INR in patients receiving warfarin

Pyrazinamide
Pyrazinamide is incorrect. Pyrazinamide is not expected to signifantly interact with warfarin.

stem: She is already taking flucloxacillin and clindamycin. Which one of the following other antibiotics might you be most likely to consider?
explanation:
Ciprofloxacin
This patient has evidence of osteomyelitis, and positive blood cultures. It is likely that a combination of antimicrobials, with or without surgical debridement, would be needed to achieve effective resolution. Effective treatments against Staphylococcus aureus typically include flucloxacillin, ciprofloxacin, rifampicin, gentamicin and vancomycin. Treatment is normally for 4–6 weeks, and long-term antimicrobial therapy may be needed to prevent recurrence.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is unlikely to add additional benefit in this circumstance.

Doxycycline
Oral doxycycline has limited activity against invasive Staphylococcus aureus.

Gentamicin
Gentamicin might offer effective antimicrobial activity; however, there is evidence of pre-existing chronic kidney disease and the risk of gentamicin-induced acute kidney injury makes this a less-favoured option than ciprofloxacin.

Trimethoprim
Oral trimethoprim is unlikely to offer effective activity against Staphylococcus aureus, and would be unwise in the setting of chronic kidney disease in any case. Pressure UlcersA 74-year-old woman with a 3-year history of Parkinson’s disease managed with Ropinirole and a small dose of Levodopa comes to the clinic with deteriorating motor symptoms. In particular she is suffering severe dyskinesia, but does not want to reduce the dose of her Parkinson’s medications for fear of increasing rigidity and tremor. Examination in the clinic reveals mild tremor and well-controlled rigidity. She does however have significant dyskinesia.

stem: A 75-year-old patient with a history of dementia dies suddenly at home. A post mortem reveals her to have Lewy body dementia. What are Lewy bodies made up of?
explanation:
Alpha synuclein
Alpha-synuclein is a neural protein thought to have a role in membrane stabilisation and turnover. Abnormal aggregates of alpha-synuclein are seen within Lewy bodies in Lewy body dementia, Parkinson’s disease and multiple systems atrophy. Deposits of alpha-synuclein are also seen in some patients with Alzheimer’s disease. In Lewy body dementia, Lewy bodies are typically seen in the cortex as well as in the substantia nigra.

Beta-amyloid
Beta-amyloid is incorrect. It is best known as a component of amyloid plaques seen in Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer’s disease-type changes can be seen in Lewy body dementia, but Lewy bodies do not contain betaamyloid.

DNA inclusion bodies
DNA inclusion bodies is incorrect. These are usually known as Howell?Jolly bodies and are seen in erythrocytes, not in Lewy bodies. During maturation, the nucleus of an erythrocyte is usually expelled; however, sometimes this does not occur and instead some DNA remains in clusters within the cytoplasm. This cluster is termed a Howell-Jolly body. These are seen on blood films in hyposplenism.

Lipofuscin
Lipofuscin is incorrect. It is the name given to yellow/brown pigment granules found around the nucleus in ageing cells. Abnormal accumulation of lipofuscin is seen in specific and rare neurodegenerative diseases, but is also seen in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease. However, lipofuscin is not found within Lewy bodies.

Tau protein
Tau protein is incorrect. Tau protein can become pathologically hyperphosphorylated and form neurofibrillary tangles, which are a key finding in patients with Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. Tau protein does not occur within Lewy bodies.

stem: An elderly man on medical ward was being prepared for discharge, but develops severe joint pain in his left ankle and left knee, with swelling and redness. The reason for his admission was heart failure. Blood tests show a normal white cell count and urate. His CRP is elevated at 45mg/l. Which investigation would be the most important in making a diagnosis?
explanation:
Joint fluid microscopy
Gouty arthritis may be precipitated by diuretic therapy (treatment for heart failure). Joint fluid microscopy would show the presence of long, needle-shaped uric acid crystals that are negatively birefringent under plane polarised light.

ESR
ESR is incorrect. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) estimation would not provide a diagnosis.

Joint fluid culture
Joint fluid culture is incorrect. The joint fluid would be sterile (although joint fluid culture is indicated to exclude infection).

Rheumatoid factor
Rheumatoid factor is incorrect. This is not likely to be rheumatoid arthritis, as has occurred post-diuresis and RA is a small joint polyarthritis.

X-ray ankle
X-ray ankle is incorrect. An X-ray is unlikely to show any changes and should not be requested immediately unless a fracture is suspected.

stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted to hospital with palpitations. A resting ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rate 107/min. You decide to prescribe digoxin therapy. Which of the following most accurately describes the pharmacological mechanism of action of digoxin?
options: Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
explanation:
Inhibition of sodium-potassium ATPase
The key pharmacological mechanism is inhibition of Na +/K + ATPase, which is located in the sarcolemmal membrane. This causes accumulation of intracellular sodium and calcium by way of the sodium–calcium exchange mechanism; intracellular potassium concentrations decrease whereas extracellular potassium concentrations increase. Digitalis glycosides increase the contractility of the heart (positively inotropic) and decrease the resting heart rate (negatively chronotropic) and delay A–V nodal conduction.

Opening of calcium channels
Opening of calcium channels is incorrect. Intracellular calcium concentrations increase, but there is no direct action of digoxin on cardiac calcium channels.

Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is incorrect. Calcium concentrations increase due to sodium–calcium exchange, rather than release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Stimulation of membrane phospholipase C
Stimulation of membrane phospholipase C is incorrect. Digoxin is not known to exert a direct effect on phospholipase C. Many other receptor systems act via phospholipase C, including 5-HT2 serotonergic, α1 adrenergic, calcitonin, H1 histamine, glutamate receptors, and M1, M3 and M5 muscarinic receptors.

Stimulation of myosin ATPase
Stimulation of myosin ATPase is incorrect. The effect is inhibition rather than stimulation of the Na +/K + ATPase.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful intervention?
explanation:
Plasma exchange
Plasma exchange is the most useful intervention. This lady has been affected by food poisoning, along with other residents in the same home. One of the other residents has had acute renal impairment. This lady has a purpuric rash, which is associated with her thrombocytopaenia. In addition she is anaemic, with a normal white cell count. She has evidence of worsening renal impairment and she also has neurological signs in that she has left-sided weakness. The possibility of thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP) is raised, given this history, the physical findings and the lab results. This is associated with a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, when there is anaemia and thrombocytopaenia for no other apparent reason. There was also evidence of acute kidney disease, which is seen in TTP. There are also neurological signs in TTP as in this patient. The best treatment for TTP is plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma.

Eculizumab
Eculizumab is incorrect. Eculizumab is a treatment that is used on PNH and is a monoclonal antibody against complement. It is used in the treatment of TTP, but usually only where it is refractory to other interventions.

FFP
FFP is incorrect. A simple infusion with plasma in the form of FFP is less efficacious than plasma exchange in this situation. Where there is focal neurological deficit, plasma exchange can significantly neurological outcomes.

IV ciprofloxacin
IV ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This lady needs plasma exchange with FFP as her main treatment. Some studies suggest that quinolones in this case to combat E coli infection may actually worsen outcomes.

IV corticosteroids
IV corticosteroids is incorrect. IV corticosteroids again can be used as adjunctive treatment in TTP, but plasma exchange with FFP is the primary treatment required. Data on use of corticosteroids is conflicting, with limited evidence of benefit.

stem: A 72-year-old ex-soldier who has spent significant amounts of time in Africa presents to the Emergency Department due to an ulcer over his left shin, which has grown in size over the past 4 years. Past history of note is that he has had a number of actinic keratoses removed from his head, varicose veins, and type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin. On examination, he has a large, shiny ulcerating lesion on his left shin. It is 3cm in diameter and has rolled, raised edges. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Basal cell carcinoma
The history of significant sun exposure, coupled with a shiny, slow-growing lesion occurring on sun-exposed skin, with rolled raised edges fits best with a basal cell carcinoma. Bearing in mind this lesion is on his shin, excision may be technically challenging and therefore punch biopsy to confirm the diagnosis is often considered before excision. Radiotherapy may be performed instead if complete surgical excision is likely to lead to an unfavourable outcome with poor wound healing (e.g. due to poor circulation).

Keratoacanthoma
Keratoacanthoma is incorrect. Keratoacanthomas tend to be rapidly growing lesions which erupt in sundamaged skin and that usually resolve spontaneously within a few weeks, leaving behind a small area of scarring. The history of slow growth and ulceration makes the diagnosis of keratoacanthoma unlikely.

Necrobiosis lipoidica
Necrobiosis lipoidica is incorrect. Necrobiosis lipoidica is a rare granulomatous skin disorder of unknown cause which can affect the shin of insulin-dependent diabetics, but may occur in non-diabetic patients as well. Clinically, it is associated with yellowish, atrophic lesions with telangiectasia that develop slowly over months.

Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is incorrect. This is a subtype of melanoma that does not produce melanin. Clinically, it presents as an enlarging flesh-coloured, pink or red nodule that is prone to bleeding and ulceration. The atypical presentation leads to delays in diagnosis and treatment and is therefore associated with a poor prognosis.

Venous leg ulcer
Venous leg ulcer is incorrect. Venous leg ulcers occur due to poor circulation and pooling of venous blood in the lower legs. They commonly occur in the gaiter area over the medial malleoli and are associated with signs of venous stasis such as lipodermatosclerosis, venous eczema and haemosiderin deposition.

stem: An 87-year-old man has had a dementing illness for the past 7 years. He is looked after at home by his daughter, and requires help with all his activities of daily living (ADL). His last CT scan showed severe, diffuse, cerebral atrophy. On his previous assessment at the Neurology Clinic the cause of his dementia was felt to be Alzheimer’s disease. His Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score is 8/30. He has a previous history of renal stones and hypertension. His daughter has read about the ‘drug treatment for dementia’ and wishes to know if he is eligible for this. What is the main reason for his not being suitable for an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor?
options: His past history of renal stones
explanation:
His MMSE score
Acetylcholinesterase-inhibiting drugs (donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine) have been licensed for the treatment of ‘mild to moderate’ Alzheimer’s disease – as per NICE guidance. The guidelines state that relying solely on a cognitive measure such as the MMSE for grading dementia severity should be avoided. However, in this case an MMSE of < 10/30 in someone who requires full assistance with ADLs would be classified as severe dementia. Thus, the MMSE score is the best answer to help provide a cutoff for these drugs. Currently, a drug called memantine could be prescribed in this situation, as it is currently approved for use in ‘severe’ Alzheimer’s disease.

His age
His age is incorrect. Age is not a reason to withhold medication.

His past history of hypertension
His past history of hypertension is incorrect. There is no contraindication for these medications with respect to hypertension, although care must be taken if there is a cardiac disease history as the drugs predispose to bradycardia and heart block.

His past history of renal stones
His past history of renal stones is incorrect. There is no contraindication for these medications with respect to renal stones.

The duration of his illness
The duration of his illness is incorrect. Duration of illness is not a reason to withhold medication.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism currently treated with thyroxine replacement presents with gradually progressive weakness over the past few months. She now finds it difficult to get out of a chair and to climb the stairs at home. Medication includes thyroxine and ramipril. On examination her BP is 138/88 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. She has fatigable ptosis and proximal myopathy affecting both the upper and lower limbs. There is no muscle wasting or fasciculation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myasthenia gravis
In a patient with slowly progressive proximal myopathy, and who already has a history of autoimmunity, myasthenia gravis (MG) is a possibility. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness and ptosis. There is no muscle wasting or fasciculation. Tone is normal. Sensation is unimpaired and tendon reflexes are normal. Antiacetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in 85% of patients with generalised myasthenia, although antibody positivity is less in patients with ocular myasthenia. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, combined with oral corticosteroids, are the mainstay of therapy.

Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is incorrect. Myotonic dystrophy presents with muscle weakness and myotonia. It normally presents in the 20s or 30s, so a first presentation of myotonic dystrophy at the age of 71 would be very unlikely.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease presents with weakness, muscle wasting and fasciculations. The lack of wasting and fasciculations in this case makes a diagnosis of motor neurone disease unlikely.

Guillain-Barré syndrome
Guillain-Barré syndrome is incorrect. Guillain-Barré syndrome usually presents with weakness. In 60% of cases onset occurs approximately three weeks after a viral illness. The condition usually presents with an ascending pattern of progressive symmetrical weakness, starting in the lower extremities. Neuropathic pain may develop, and reflexes may be reduced or absent.

Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is incorrect. Lambert-Eaton is most commonly seen in association with bronchial carcinoma. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness, which may initially on exercise but then lessens as exercise is sustained. Reflexes are also reduced or absent.

stem: Which of the following medications is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Indapamide
Indapamide is commonly prescribed for hypertension in the elderly and is associated with both hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia. The hyponatraemia could explain her confusion, particularly if the onset has been fairly sudden.

Amiloride
Amiloride is incorrect. Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that may cause hyperkalaemia.

Bumetanide
Bumetanide is incorrect. Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that can cause hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia. It is not, however, used as a treatment for hypertension, and given this patient has no history of frank heart failure, it is unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s biochemistry.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Furosemide is a loop diuretic that can cause hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia, however, it is not used as a treatment for hypertension and, therefore, would not fit with the clinical picture seen here.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is incorrect. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic, and as such results in hyperkalaemia.

stem: Within a few weeks several patients in a geriatric ward contracted a Legionella pneumonia, which has been successfully treated with macrolide antibiotics. What was the most likely source of those nosocomial infections?
explanation:
Contaminated warm-water source
This is a ‘know it or you don’t’ question. Legionella organisms have been found in small numbers in water distribution systems, through which they can colonise man-made habitats, again as part of the biofilm from which they are shed into the water. Factors that encourage colonisation and multiplication are temperature (20– 45 °C) and stagnation. The most common sources in buildings in which Legionella organisms have been found are: Hot-water calorifiers Storage tanks Piped water, especially hot water from the calorifiers in large buildings and industrial complexes with long runs of pipework. Other well-recognised sources include: Recirculating water in air-conditioning and cooling systems Whirlpool spas and other warm-water baths Decorative fountains Nebulisers and humidifier reservoirs of hospital ventilation machines if topped up with contaminated tap water. Dissemination of infection is by contaminated water droplets (aerosol), which are inhaled. To cause infection the droplets must be of a size that can reach the alveoli of the lungs (less than 5 mm in diameter). Taps and shower-heads produce very localised aerosols, whereas the water droplets (drift) contained in the airstream released from a cooling tower can be carried a considerable distance and expose a greater number of people to risk.

Contaminated instruments
Contaminated instruments is incorrect. Transmission via contaminated instruments would be a less likely source of infection than a contaminated warm-water source.

Contaminated medication boxes
Contaminated medication boxes is incorrect. Contaminated medication boxes would be a less likely source of infection than a contaminated warm-water source.

Droplet transmission from staff
Droplet transmission from staff is incorrect. Droplet transmission from staff would be a less likely source of infection than a contaminated warm-water source.

Insufficient hand disinfection
Insufficient hand disinfection is incorrect. Insufficient hand disinfection would be a less likely source of infection than a contaminated warm-water source. Legionella A 78-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with confusion. She apparently takes a number of different anti-hypertensive medications, but these were not brought with her to the Emergency Department. On examination she is clearly confused, her BP is 135/75 mmHg, pulse 75 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender and her BMI is 23. Investigations.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with worsening back pain. She also feels generally weak. An X-ray of her back shows multiple vertebral collapses and lytic lesions. Given the likely clinical diagnosis, what is the most appropriate therapy for her underlying condition?
explanation:
Chemotherapy
The most likely clinical diagnosis here is multiple myeloma due to the lytic lesions. Combination chemotherapy is the most appropriate initial therapy for her underlying condition. This is usually a thalidomide containing regime with steroids, such as the CTD regimen (cyclophosphamide, thalidomide and dexamethasone), or MPT regime (melphalan, prednisone and thalidomide). Please note detailed knowledge of chemotherapy regimens is not required at MRCP level; broad principles are much more important.

Bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates is incorrect. Bisphosphonates are not the most appropriate therapy for the underlying condition, but are crucial in supportive treatment of myeloma, to strengthen bone by encouraging bone formation. There is also some evidence to suggest that they have an anti-myeloma effect in their own right.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids are given in conjunction with chemotherapy as described above however corticosteroids are not the most appropriate therapy unless there is evidence of cord compression.

Radiotherapy
Radiotherapy is incorrect. Radiotherapy is not the most appropriate initial therapy unless there is evidence of cord compression.

Splenectomy
Splenectomy is incorrect. Splenectomy is not part of myeloma therapy. It may be required for the following reasons: hemolytic anemia thalassemia acute leukemia chronic myeloid or lymphocytic leukemia lymphoma polycythemia vera immune thrombocytopenic purpura Felty syndrome portal hypertension amyloidosis Gaucher disease splenic trauma.

stem: A 76-year-old man comes to a well man check as he has suffered two episodes of syncope in the past 3 weeks and is feeling increasingly tired. On examination his pulse is 40/min and his BP 100/60 mmHg. An ECG reveals he is in complete heart block. What other finding are you most likely to find?
explanation:
Variable S1
Complete heart block means no relationship between the timing of atrial and ventricular contraction. Blood flow from the atria to the ventricles will thus vary beat to beat, resulting in variable intensity of the first heart sound (closure of the atrioventricular (AV) valves). In addition cannon A waves may be seen in the neck, suggesting atrial contraction against closed AV valves

Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is incorrect. Aortic stenosis is not classically associated with complete heart block. It does lead to reversed splitting of S2.

Giant v wave
Giant v wave is incorrect. Giant v waves in contrast suggest tricuspid regurgitation.

Narrow pulse pressure
Narrow pulse pressure is incorrect. Narrow pulse pressure would suggest aortic valve disease.

Reversed splitting of S2
Reversed splitting of S2 is incorrect. Reversed splitting of S2 is found in aortic stenosis (AS), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) and left bundle branch block (LBBB). It is worth noting that a range of murmurs are possible in CHB as concomitant valve disease is more common.

stem: An 82-year-old white woman has short history of bone pain. Serum biochemistry reveals: plasma calcium concentration 2.08 mmol/l, phosphate 0.70 mmol/l, alkaline phosphatase activity twice the upper limit of normal. The concentration of parathyroid hormone is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is most frequently related to lack or impaired metabolism of vitamin D. Hypocalcaemia might not be striking because of increased parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which also increases renal phosphate excretion; the elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity. In this situation measurement of vitamin D is most appropriate, with supplementation when low levels are confirmed.

Osteolytic metastases
Osteolytic metastases is incorrect. Plasma alkaline phosphatase is often increased in patients with osteolytic secondaries, but the calcium concentration is in the normal range or elevated rather than being just below the lower limit of normal here.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. In uncomplicated osteoporosis, bone markers are all in the normal range, although when there is a fracture or prolonged bed rest, alkaline phosphatase and calcium may be elevated.

Renal osteodystrophy
Renal osteodystrophy is incorrect. Plasma phosphate concentration is increased in renal osteodystrophy because of the underlying kidney disease.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Although hypophosphataemia is characteristic of primary hyperparathyroidism, plasma calcium concentration is usually elevated (an exception is when there is concomitant vitamin D deficiency).

stem: A 72-year-old woman is treated with oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Her creatinine was checked on the first day of therapy and found to be 122 μmol/l; after 5 days her renal function is re-assessed and the creatinine has risen to 142 μmol/l. Which of the following is the reason for this?
options: Antagonism of the distal tubular epithelial sodium channel
explanation:
Competitive inhibition of creatinine secretion
Creatinine is a cation in the physiologic pH range and is secreted by the organic cation secretory pump, and this can be inhibited by other organic cations. A number of commonly used drugs can interfere with creatinine secretion leading to a self-limiting and reversible rise in serum creatinine without changing the true GFR, for example, trimethoprim and cimetidine.

Antagonism of the distal tubular epithelial sodium channel
Antagonism of the distal tubular epithelial sodium channel is incorrect. Trimethoprim does interfere with the action of the distal tubular epithelial sodium channel, but this causes hyperkalaemia rather than increased creatinine.

Decreased renal perfusion
Decreased renal perfusion is incorrect. Trimethoprim has no direct effect on renal blood flow.

Increased sodium and water excretion
Increased sodium and water excretion is incorrect. Trimethoprim does not directly alter sodium or water elimination.

Non-competitive inhibition of creatinine secretion
Non-competitive inhibition of creatinine secretion is incorrect. It causes competitive inhibition, so that the effect is dose-dependent.

stem: A 74-year-old man with extensive metastases related to prostatic carcinoma comes to the Emergency Department with dysphagia. Apparently, the problem has increased significantly over the last few days and he is now unable to drink without choking. Neurological examination reveals an absent gag reflex, weakness of the neck and a hoarse voice. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Jugular foramen
The cranial nerves which pass through the jugular foramen ((IX, X and XI) and the internal jugular vein can become compromised by a lesion causing jugular foramen syndrome. Nerve IX (glossopharyngeal) receives sensory fibres from the tonsils, pharynx, middle ear and posterior 1/3 of the tongue. It also supplies motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus muscle. Nerve X (vagus) has both sympathetic and parasympathetic functions. In addition, it supplies motor fibres to several of the muscles in the palate and pharynx. Finally, nerve XI (accessory) provides motor control of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

Broca's area
Broca’s area is incorrect. Broca's area is a region in the frontal lobe of the dominant hemisphere (usually the left), which is responsible for the production of speech. Lesions in that area present with expressive aphasia.

Geniculate ganglion
Geniculate ganglion is incorrect. The geniculate ganglion is one of several ganglia of the head and neck and receives motor, sensory and parasympathetic fibres of the facial nerve. Lesions in that region can present with facial nerve palsy and hearing loss.

Internal capsule
Internal capsule is incorrect. Axons that originate in the motor cortex traverse the internal capsule. Therefore, lesions in this area present as contralateral hemiplegia.

Thalamus
Thalamus is incorrect. Lesions affecting the thalamus (most commonly secondary to stroke) present with contralateral numbness, dysaesthesia, allodynia and tingling.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife. She is worried that he has loss of short term memory and has increasingly inappropriate mood swings and hallucinations. Apparently he used to box and was an amateur footballer. You are considering a diagnosis of frontal lobe dementia. Which of the following would drive you most towards a differential of frontal lobe dementia versus other causes?
explanation:
Failure to draw interlocking pentagons
Constructional apraxia, or the inability to draw complex figures, localises any potential lesion to either the right hemisphere or the frontal lobes.

Depression screen
Depression screen is incorrect. Depression may co-exist with a number of forms of dementia, and therefore high scores on a depression screen are not differentiating versus dementia.

Early severe memory deficit
Early severe memory deficit is incorrect. Early severe memory deficit is more likely to be seen in CreutzfeldtJakob disease (CJD) than in frontal lobe dementia, and memory is well preserved in the early stages of frontal lobe dementia.

Lack of symptoms of incontinence
Lack of symptoms of incontinence is incorrect. Early incontinence may be seen in frontal dementia due to involvement of the anterior cingulate gyrus.

Mini-mental state examination overall score
Mini mental state examination overall score is incorrect. The MMSE score may be low in both dementia and depression and hence is not of value as a differentiator.

stem: You review a 78-year-old man who was admitted with hypotension and tachycardia and is found to have atrial fibrillation. The admitting FY2 diagnosed sepsis and commenced him on gentamicin therapy. He is on multiple drugs, including fluoxetine for depression, bumetanide for fluid overload, amiodarone for atrial fibrillation and diazepam to help him sleep. You wish to adjust some of his existing medications and add new treatments. Which of the following medications if stopped, would take longest for adverse effects to resolve?
explanation:
Amiodarone
Amiodarone has by far the longest half-life of these agents, at around 25–30 days. Initiation of therapy requires a loading regimen over the first few weeks of treatment, and cessation may take several months before drug concentrations have fallen to an insignificant level. The half-life is dependent upon lipid solubility and wide distribution of the drug to extravascular tissues. With wide volume of distribution and extensive tissue binding there is slow renal or hepatic drug clearance.

Bumetanide
Bumetanide is incorrect. Bumetanide has a short half-life, around 1 h, so the effects are comparatively shortlived.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Diazepam is highly lipid soluble, which helps it cross the blood–brain barrier; the plasma half-life is around 43 h, although the biological effects may persist for longer due to persistence in the brain tissue.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. Fluoxetine is very lipid-soluble and has a comparatively long half-life of around 50 h. Irrespective of the half-life, the biological response to starting or stopping therapy may take 2–3 weeks (that is, a dissociation between the pharmacokinetic profile and pharmacodynamic actions).

Gentamicin
Gentamicin is incorrect. Gentamicin is water soluble and clearance is highly dependent upon renal excretion; in patients with normal renal function the half-life of gentamicin is around 2–3 h.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe pneumonia, hypotension and signs of sepsis. There is a history of previous GP attendance for a urinary tract infection. According to her husband, she has been prescribed a prolonged course of co-trimoxazole, as this has been her third urinary infection in the past 2 months. She has had diarrhoea and vomiting for the past 24 h. Her total white blood count is 1.8 × 10 9/litre, and neutrophil count is 0.2 × 10 9/litre. What is the most likely explanation for these laboratory findings?
explanation:
Neutropaenia secondary to co-trimoxazole therapy
Co-trimoxazole is now only indicated for oral prophylaxis against pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis and nocardiosis due to the risk of neutropaenia. It is effective against a number of organisms that cause respiratory and urinary infections, but should normally only be considered where there is no other safer alternative. Adverse effects include nausea, rash, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, neutropaenia, thrombocytopaenia and photosensitivity. It should be avoided or used with caution in patients with renal or hepatic impairment.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia
Chronic myeloid leukaemia is incorrect. A hallmark of chronic myeloid leukaemia is production of high numbers of leukocytes, not neutropaenia, albeit that they are often dysfunctional and render patientsChat susceptible to with infection.

Salmonella infection
Salmonella infection is incorrect. Salmonella infection may be associated with leukopaenia and neutropaenia, although it would be very rare for the white count to be suppressed to the low levels reported here.

Severe pneumonia
Severe pneumonia is incorrect. Overwhelming bacterial infection may be associated with leukopaenia and neutropaenia, although it would be very rare for the white count to be suppressed to the low levels reported here.

Urinary tract infection with sepsis
Urinary tract infection with sepsis is incorrect. Overwhelming bacterial infection may be associated with leukopaenia and neutropaenia, although it would be very rare for the white count to be suppressed to the low levels reported here. NeutropeniaA 72-year-old man with known metastases as a result of disseminated prostate cancer comes to the Emergency Department for review with increased tiredness. Despite hormonal therapy, his PSA has risen slowly over the past few months, and he has required a blood transfusion some 3 months ago. On examination, his BP is 105/70 mmHg; pulse is 95/min and regular. He looks pale and is complaining of pain in his lower back and right femur. A bone scan report from some 4 months ago reveals extensive bony metastases. The Hb on the blood gas machine is 81 g/l.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden onset of right arm weakness and slurred speech that resolved within 30 minutes. His past medical history includes hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidaemia. He is currently on aspirin, metformin, atorvastatin and lisinopril. What is the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Carotid artery stenosis
Carotid artery stenosis is a common cause of transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs), especially in elderly patients with risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia. The transient nature of his symptoms suggests a temporary reduction in blood flow to part of the brain, which often results from an embolus originating from a narrowed carotid artery. Imaging studies such as Doppler ultrasound or magnetic resonance angiography can help confirm this diagnosis by visualising the degree of stenosis present in the carotid arteries. Management typically involves antiplatelet therapy and possibly surgical intervention, depending on the severity of the stenosis.

AF
AF can lead to embolic strokes but would more commonly cause persistent rather than transient neurological deficits. Additionally, there was no mention of irregular heart rhythm during examination or prior episodes suggesting paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

Lacunar infarction
Lacunar infarction usually results from small vessel disease affecting deeper brain structures rather than cortical areas supplied by larger vessels like carotids. Therefore it tends not to present withChat transient with AIischaemic Tutor attacks but instead with small strokes causing persistent focal deficits without changes seen on initial imaging.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis primarily affects younger individuals (20-40 years old), presenting with relapsing-remitting neurological deficits including optic neuritis or sensory disturbances over days/weeks rather than minutes/hours typical for transient ischaemic attacks due to vascular causes.

Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis rarely causes transient ischaemic attacks. It predominantly affects older adults causing headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication due to inflammation in temporal arteries plus elevated inflammatory markers like ESR/CRP aiding diagnosis alongside temporal artery biopsy confirmation.

stem: He is admitted to the high dependency unit, and you are asked to see him at 2am as he has become acutely confused and aggressive, saying the nurses are trying to poison him and a priest has visited to perform an exorcism. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Delirium
The information we are provided with suggests this man has a good pre-morbid functional status and lives independently. As such we are looking for an acute cause of confusion as the most likely answer here. Urinary tract infection with bacterial sepsis is the most likely underlying aetiology, and the alien surroundings of the HDU are likely to have exacerbated his agitation. Supportive nursing, rather than sedation, is the cornerstone of management.

Acute paranoid schizophrenia
Acute paranoid schizophrenia is incorrect. Acute schizophrenia is highly unlikely to present for the first time at the age of 82, although paraphrenia may present in older patients with hearing impairment. Features consistent with schizophrenia apart from delusions are also absent.

Dementia
Dementia is incorrect. Given he usually lives alone and there is no history of deterioration with respect to his ability to remain independent, delirium is much more lkely.

TIA
TIA is incorrect. A transcient ischemic attack (TIA) without focal neurology, only leading to behavioural change is very unlikely.

Temporal lobe epilepsy
Temporal lobe epilepsy is incorrect. Temporal lobe epilepsy usually presents with episodes of loss of consciousness and automatisms.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a ten-month history of progressively worsening hearing loss in both ears. She also reports experiencing tinnitus and occasional dizziness but denies any ear pain or discharge. On examination, there is no evidence of external or middle ear pathology, and Rinne's test is positive bilaterally, while Weber's test lateralises to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)
Presbycusis is characterised by bilateral sensorineural hearing loss that progresses gradually over time, which fits this patient's presentation perfectly. The positive Rinne’s test bilaterally indicates that air conduction is better than bone conduction in both ears, consistent with sensorineural deafness typical of presbycusis. The lateralisation of Weber’s test to the right suggests either more significant conductive loss on the left side or better cochlear function on the right side.

Acoustic neuroma
While acoustic neuroma can cause unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and balance issues, it typically presents with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss rather than bilateral involvement as seen in this patient. Additionally, the absence of facial nerve involvement makes this diagnosis less likely.

Chronic otitis media
Chronic otitis media usually presents with symptoms such as persistent ear discharge (otorrhoea), recurrent infections and often some degree of conductive hearing loss due to middle ear pathology which was not evident during examination in this patient.

Ménière’s disease
Although Ménière's disease can present with tinnitus and episodic vertigo alongside fluctuating hearing loss, it typically affects one ear initially rather than causing bilateral symptoms from onset as described here.

Otosclerosis
Otosclerosis generally leads to progressive conductive hearing loss due to abnormal bone growth around the stapes footplate but does not usually present bilaterally at first without a family history suggestive of early onset cases; it also tends not to involve significant dizziness unless advanced stages are reached, affecting vestibular structures indirectly through inner ear changes.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with episodes of dizziness and syncope over the past month. His ECG reveals a complete heart block. What is the most likely next step in management?
explanation:
Implantation of a permanent pacemaker
Implantation of a permanent pacemaker is indeed the best next step for managing a patient with complete heart block. Complete heart block signifies that there is no transmission of electrical signals from the atria to the ventricles, which can lead to severe bradycardia and hemodynamic instability. A permanent pacemaker restores synchronized cardiac contractions by providing reliable pacing stimuli to maintain adequate heart rate and cardiac output, significantly reducing symptoms such as dizziness or syncope.

Beta-blockers
Beta-blockers are typically used to manage various cardiovascular conditions, including hypertension and arrhythmias. However, they are contraindicated in patients with complete heart block as they can exacerbate bradycardia by further inhibiting atrioventricular node conduction. In this scenario, beta-blockers would not address the fundamental issue of impaired electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles.

Observation and follow-up
Observation and follow-up might be appropriate for other types of heart block or situations where transient factors contribute to bradycardia; however, complete heart block requires more definitive intervention due to its potential for causing life-threatening complications like severe hypotension or ventricular arrhythmias.

Digoxin
Prescription of digoxin could be considered in certain types of supraventricular tachyarrhythmias but is not suitable for treating complete heart block. Digoxin primarily increases vagal tone on AV node conduction which could worsen an already compromised atrioventricular node function leading to further reductions in ventricular rate.

Thrombolytic therapy
Thrombolytic therapy is normally indicated for acute embolic events when interventional procedures can not be performed in a timely manner. It would be unlikely to be required for complete heart block unless it was secondary to an acute embolic event leading to ischemic changes resulting in atrioventricular nodal disease. This treatment is unlikely to be the next step in management without other clinical evidence indicating acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

stem: A 65-year-old man is due his annual vaccinations. Against which one of the following pathogens is immunisation most likely to be given on a yearly basis to this patient?
explanation:
Influenza virus
There is currently no vaccine available for disease due to L. pneumophila. Influenza vaccination represents one of the most important health promotion and disease prevention measures in the elderly population. Annual vaccination is currently recommended for all persons over the age of 65. At highest risk are those elderly individuals with underlying chronic diseases, particularly those with cardiorespiratory disorders and metabolic or neoplastic diseases. Although influenza vaccination is recognised as perhaps the most cost-effective medical intervention in the elderly population, protection rates are reduced from approximately 90% in younger adults to anywhere between 25% and 44% in the elderly population. The vaccination does not change the incidence of upper respiratory tract infection, but significantly reduces hospital admission and mortality rates by 72% and 87%, respectively, in community-dwelling elderly people. The efficacy is greatly reduced in nursing home residents, who tend to have a greater burden of chronic disease, such that there may be effectively no difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated residents in long-term care.

Varicella zoster virus
Shingles, which is caused by the varicella zoster virus, is vaccinated against in patients agedChat between to 79. with AI 70 Tutor Therefore, this patient would not fit into the correct age bracket for this intervention.

Legionella pneumophila
Legionella pneumophila is incorrect. There is currently no vaccine available for disease due to L. pneumophila.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. It is recommended that individuals over 65 years of age are vaccinated against pneumococcal disease with the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (which is different from the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine used for infants), but individuals require only one dose, which provides lifelong immunity. Adults under 65 years may also require vaccination if they are particularly at risk; for example, if they are HIV-positive or have other chronic diseases.

Neisseria meningitidis
Neisseria meningitidis is incorrect. Meningococcal vaccines are given routinely to infants, children and adults with asplenia, splenic dysfunction or complement disorders. Routine use in the over-65s is not recommended.

stem: Which other clinical finding is most likely in this case?
explanation:
Petechiae/ecchymoses
Petechiae/ecchymosis would be the other most likely clinical finding of those listed. This lady has a raised white cell count and raised platelet count, associated with massive splenomegaly. She is likely to have an underlying myeloproliferative condition, such as myelofibrosis, or possibly chronic myeloid leukemia. Both conditions can be associated with disordered platelet function, resulting in petechiae or ecchymosis.

Ascites
Ascites is incorrect. Ascites is not a common finding in myeloproliferative conditions.

Hepatomegaly
Hepatomegaly is incorrect. Hepatomegaly can occur in association with myeloproliferative disorders, but it is a more variable sign than petechiae or ecchymosis.

Inguinal lymphadenopathy
Inguinal lymphadenopathy is incorrect. Inguinal lymphadenopathy would be more likely to be seen in lymphoproliferative disorders.

Lymphoedema
Lymphoedema is incorrect. Lymphoedema is not associated with myeloproliferative disorders.

stem: An 83-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe shortness of breath and palpitations. He said these began abruptly around 5 h ago. There is a past history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril and amlodipine, and asthma for which he takes a seretide inhaler. On examination, his BP is 80/60 mmHg, pulse 155/min (atrial fibrillation). There are coarse crackles on auscultation of the chest consistent with LVF. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage him?
explanation:
DC cardioversion
This man is hypotensive with signs of left ventricular failure. Given that we have a defined point of onset of AF some 5 h earlier, the chances of embolic phenomena are low and therefore DC cardioversion is considered the best option.

IV amiodarone
IV amiodarone is incorrect. Chemical cardioversion with amiodarone would only be an option if he was cardiovascularly stable.

IV digoxin
IV digoxin is incorrect. IV digoxin is good for rate control in atrial fibrillation, but would not be the most appropriate treatment in the face of hypotension and heart failure due to fast atrial fibrillation, where DC cardioversion should be performed.

IV verapamil
IV verapamil is incorrect. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and is an alternative for cardioversion, but again not with this degree of hypotension or cardiac failure.

Oral flecainide
Oral flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide is appropriate for paroxysmal AF only in the absence of structural heart disease.

stem: A 74-year-old man comes to the neurology clinic for review. He has become progressively more confused over the past 18 months, is now unable to go out of the house alone and has frequent mood swings. According to his wife, his mood is very labile and there are frequent violent rages. There is a past medical history of hypertension, but nil else of note. On examination his BP is 185/95 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. There are no murmurs and his chest is clear. Neurological examination reveals evidence of bradykinesia and a tremor with evidence of cogwheel rigidity, where symptoms are worse on the right than the left. Which of the following is mostly likely to point towards Lewy body disease as a diagnosis rather than other forms of dementia?
explanation:
Extreme reaction to neuroleptics
Lewy body dementia is associated with damage to dopaminergic neurones; as such, there are both symptoms of Parkinson’s disease and enhanced sensitivity to neuroleptics, which may lead to a significant deterioration in movement. Lewy body disease consists of a triad of symptoms, which are fluctuating confusion/onset of dementia, persistent visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonism. Other symptoms consistent with a diagnosis of Lewy body disease include REM sleep disorder and unexplained syncope.

Daytime somnolence
Daytime somnolence is incorrect. It is not unique to Lewy body disease, as this is also present in dementia patients.

Evidence of vascular disease
Evidence of vascular disease is incorrect. This would point to a diagnosis of vascular or mixed-type dementia.

Mini-mental state examination <15
Mini-mental state examination <15 is incorrect. MMSE scores tend to be preserved earlier on in the disease process of Lewy body dementia. It would be more common to see lower scores in Alzheimer’s disease.

Preserved backwards counting
Preserved backwards counting is incorrect. Backwards counting is lost early on in Lewy body disease.

stem: A 76-year-old residential home resident is brought into the Emergency Department increasingly drowsy. She has had worsening of short-term memory over the last few days and today she was too drowsy to get out of bed. She has mild dementia and is taking only an antihypertensive and a statin. She has no drug allergies. On examination, she has a GCS score of 12 and is febrile at 38.2 °C. Her chest X-ray and urine dipstick are unremarkable. She appears to have a rather stiff neck. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Ceftriaxone, amoxicillin and aciclovir
This question requires knowledge of the causative agents of meningitis in different age groups. Although all age groups should be covered for meningococcal and pneumococcal disease, the elderly are at increased risk of Listeria meningitis. This presents in a similar manner to other causes of bacterial meningitis, although all causes can present more atypically in the elderly and consequently meningitis should be considered in any elderly patient with fever and disturbance of their mental state. Ceftriaxone should adequately cover meningococcus and pneumococcus, but guidelines recommend adding in amoxicillin for patients at increased risk of Listeria infection (aged over 60 or those who are immunosuppressed). Aciclovir should be added due to the possibility of viral meningitis.

Ceftriaxone
This is a 76-year-old patient who is at risk of Listeria meningitis, so this should be covered in treatment. Ceftriaxone alone does not give adequate cover.

Ceftriaxone with aciclovir
The patient is 76 years old. Therefore, coverage for Listeria, including amoxicillin, must be added in the management plan.

Ceftriaxone with vancomycin
Vancomycin may be used if there is particular concern about resistant pneumococcal strains. They are currently relatively rare in the UK but may require cover in the context of recent travel to an at-risk area.

Chloramphenicol
Chloramphenicol would be the agent of choice in place of ceftriaxone if there is a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. Chloramphenicol is usually used as a topical treatment for bacterial conjunctivitis, as well as for otitis externa.

stem: A 70-year-old man suffers a large stroke with left-sided hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopia, left-sided neglect, receptive dysphasia and poor left-sided coordination. Two weeks later his hemiparesis has improved significantly. Which of the features of his stroke is most likely to hinder further progress in rehabilitation?
explanation:
Receptive dysphasia
Significant receptive dysphasia is likely to significantly hinder recovery from stroke due to difficulties complying with rehabilitation therapy. This may hinder recovery of other aspects of disability, as cooperation with the physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech and language therapists and other MDT members is key.

Residual hemiparesis
Residual hemiparesis is incorrect. Weakness can gradually and over time and, with the help of a physiotherapist, this can significantly in some patients.

Neglect
Neglect is incorrect. When patients are managed in a specialist stroke unit, recovery from neglect is excellent and most achieve a reasonable outcome with respect to function of the affected limb.

Poor coordination
Poor coordination is incorrect. There is a good chance that coordination will with practice and physiotherapy.

Homonymous hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia is incorrect. Whilst homonymous hemianopia will impact on activities such as driving, with suitable optometrist support it should not significantly impact on other activities of daily living.

stem: You review an 83-year-old woman who presents to the Emergency Department with collapse. She lives at home but has full-time carers, one of whom has accompanied her to hospital. There is a 2-day history of severe diarrhoea, fever and abdominal cramps; she has had little to no oral intake for the previous 24 hours, and that evening had collapsed on her way to the bathroom. She has a history of hypertension and diet-controlled Type 2 diabetes; she had been seen by her local GP 2 weeks previously for a lower respiratory tract infection and had completed a 5-day course of oral antibiotics. On examination she is drowsy and seems confused, but is responding to voice; she is tachycardic (133/min), tachypnoeic (28/min) and hypotensive (92/63 mmHg), with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor; her abdomen is soft but diffusely tender. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following drugs is she most likely to have recently been prescribed?
explanation:
Co-amoxiclav
This patient most likely has diarrhoea due to Clostridium difficile. The ‘4 Cs’ is a way to remember the oral antibiotics most likely to cause C. difficile diarrhoea (although this list is by no means exhaustive): clindamycin, co-amoxiclav, cephalosporins, and ciprofloxacin; intravenous cephalosporins are also associated. The bacterium produces two toxins: A, an enterotoxin; and B, which is cytotoxic and leads to bloody diarrhoea. Symptoms range from mild diarrhoea to severe colitis, when the bowel mucosa may be covered by a pseudomembrane. A severe complication is toxic megacolon, which involves inflammation of the smooth muscle layers of the colon and may lead to perforation. Antibiotic treatment of choice is with oral metronidazole or vancomycin.

Trimethoprim
Trimethoprim is incorrect. Trimethoprim and other sulphonamides do have some risk of C. difficile diarrhoea associated with them, but risks are lower than seen with use of co-amoxiclav or clarithromycin.

Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is incorrect. Nitrofurnatoin has been associated with C. difficile diarrhoea, but Co-amoxiclav has a much higher risk.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. There are risks of C. difficile diarrhoea with the use of amoxicillin, but they are not as high as with co-amoxiclav.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect. Tetracycline antibiotics are very rarely associated with C. difficile diarrhoea. Further reading NICE. Clostridium difficile infection: Risk with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Evidence Summary: Medicines and Prescribing Briefing 1 (ESMBP1). London: NICE, 2015. ( Public Health England. Clostridium difficile infection: Guidance on management and treatment. London: PHE, 2013. stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with recurrent Herpes Zoster infection. She has a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease with CKD-3 but is otherwise well. Examination reveals marked hepatosplenomegaly, and her white blood count is significantly elevated at 52, (predominantly lymphocytes). Which of the following is the most appropriate first line intervention?
explanation:
FCR combination chemotherapy
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), the diagnosis here, is characterised by an accumulation of small mature lymphocytes in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. The presenting features are persistent lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Hypogammaglobulinaemia is often present at the time of the diagnosis and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia occurs in 25% of cases. FCR combination therapy with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide and rituximab is the initial option of choice.

Alemtuzumab
Alemtuzumab is incorrect. Alemtuzumab is an anti-CD52 antibody licensed for use in patients with CLL after relapse following fludarabine therapy or where fludarabine is unsuitable or not tolerated.

Ofatumumab
Ofatumumab is incorrect. Ofatumumab is a possible treatment combined with chlorambucil in patients with untreated CLL who are not suitable for fludarabine or bendamustine.

Rituximab
Rituximab is incorrect. Rituximab alone is not recommended for the treatment of CLL because of high risk of relapse or developing treatment resistance.

Stem cell transplantation
Stem cell transplantation is incorrect. Stem cell transplantation is the only curative option, although many patients are elderly with poor functional status and unable to undergo the procedure.

stem: Which one of the following is true with respect to the best way to replace her red cells?
options: She can receive whole blood with prednisolone cover
She may receive whole blood through a white cell filter
She should receive irradiated red cells
She should receive whole blood with chlorpheniramine cover
explanation:
She should receive irradiated red cells
This lady has CLL and has been receiving a fludarabine based regimen. This is a purine analogue. All patients who receive this type of drug need to receive irradiated blood products. Fludarabine will reduce the recipient’s T-cells, making them at risk of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Irradiation of blood products will reduce this risk.

She can receive whole blood
She can receive whole blood is incorrect. Hardly anyone now needs to receive whole blood. It is always separated into individual components, namely red blood cells and platelets.

She can receive whole blood with prednisolone cover
She can receive whole blood with prednisolone cover is incorrect. Nobody receives whole blood nowadays. It is always separated into individual components, namely red blood cells and platelets.

She may receive whole blood through a white cell filter
She may receive whole blood through a white cell filter is incorrect. Nobody receives whole blood nowadays. It is always separated into individual components, namely red blood cells and platelets.

She should receive whole blood with chlorpheniramine cover
She should receive whole blood with chlorpheniramine cover is incorrect. Nobody receives whole blood nowadays. It is always separated into individual components, namely red blood cells and platelets.

stem: A 71-year-old man is treated with allopurinol for attacks of recurrent gout. He also takes a number of other therapies for the management of hypertension. Which of the following correctly represents the mode of action of allopurinol?
explanation:
Reduced urate production
The answer is reduced urate production. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that blocks successive oxidation of hypoxanthine and xanthine to produce uric acid. Accumulation of hypoxanthine and xanthine also leads to negative feedback with respect to further purine synthesis.

Increased renal urate excretion
Increased renal urate excretion is incorrect. Several drugs increase urinary elimination of urate, including probenecid and, to a lesser extent, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers.

Increased urate catabolism
Increased urate catabolism is incorrect. Increased urate catabolism is the mode of action of rasburicase, not allopurinol. Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase, which causes profound and rapid breakdown of uric acid to allantoin.

Reduced GI urate absorption
Reduced GI urate absorption is incorrect. Allopurinol has no impact on urate absorption.

Reduced urate tubular reabsorption
Reduced urate tubular reabsorption is incorrect. Allopurinol does not interfere with tubular reabsorption; aspirin and thiazide diuretics promote tubular urate reabsorption.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his aortic stenosis?
explanation:
Senile degenerative aortic stenosis
Senile degenerative aortic stenosis involves progressive calcification of the valve leaflets in response to longstanding haemodynamic stress. It is the most common cause of aortic valve replacement, usually presenting after the age of 75 years. Diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolaemia are risk factors for lesion development. Patients with senile degenerative aortic stenosis may have co-existent coronary artery disease, in which case coronary artery bypass surgery can be carried out concurrently with valve replacement.

Subacute bacterial endocarditis
Subacute bacterial endocarditis is incorrect. Subacute bacterial endocarditis presents with echocardiographic findings of an oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve or supporting structures in the path of regurgitant jets or on implanted material. It causes new-onset valvular regurgitation rather than stenosis.

Rheumatic fever
Rheumatic fever is incorrect. Rheumatic fever-related aortic stenosis tends to present in patients in their sixties.

Bicuspid aortic valve
Bicuspid aortic stenosis is incorrect. Congenital bicuspid aortic stenosis presents in patients aged 40–50 years.

Malformed tricuspid aortic valve
Malformed tricuspid aortic valve is incorrect. A Malformed tricuspid aortic valve would not be associated with aortic stenosis.

stem: A 76-year-old woman is attending the diabetic foot clinic regularly with a non-healing ulcer on her right foot. When she attends today, there is worsening cellulitis around the ulcer with offensive discharge, and she is feeling unwell in herself with a temperature of 38.3 oC. The registrar in clinic organises her admission to hospital and takes blood cultures and swabs of the ulcer. Both samples go on to grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The patient has previously had a reaction to vancomycin with a widespread rash and lip-swelling. Which one of the following antibiotics may be considered to treat her infection?
explanation:
Teicoplanin
The answer increasingly in multidrug-resistant organisms is dependent on sensitivities. However, from the agents given here, teicoplanin is the best answer. MRSA treatment in a bacteraemic patient such as described in this case is usually with vancomycin initially. However, as this patient has what sounds like a potentially serious allergy to this, then teicoplanin is a suitable alternative.
