Resistance to both of these agents does exist however, and certain strains are becoming increasingly difficult to treat. Linezolid would be another appropriate option here.

Benzylpenicillin
Benzylpenicillin is incorrect. Many streptococci are sensitive to benzylpenicillin, but the vastChat majority are with resistant, and it would not generally be used to treat any staphylococcal infection.

Flucloxacillin
Flucloxacillin is incorrect. MRSA is resistant to flucloxacillin, which would be a first choice to treat sensitive staphylococcal infections.

Gentamicin
Gentamicin is incorrect. The aminoglycosides would not usually be used first-line or in isolation to treat MRSA, and are more important in regimens targeting Gram-negative pathogens.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole may well be used in an infection caused by anaerobic bacteria, but not in MRSA. References: Gould E K, Brindle R, Chadwick P R, Fraise A P, Hill S, Nathwani D, et al. 2009. Guidelines (2008) for the prophylaxis and treatment of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections in the United Kingdom. Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy, 63, 849–861.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and hypertension is admitted to the Emergency Department after collapsing at home. According to his relative he has recently been started on oral antibiotic therapy for a lower respiratory tract infection. Other medications of note include ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, atorvastatin, aspirin, high-dose Seretide and PRN ipratropium. On examination he looks unwell, his BP is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 180/min, with runs of torsades de pointes on the ECG monitor. Which of the following antibiotics is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Clarithromycin
Both macrolides (such as clarithromycin) and quinolones (such as ciprofloxacin), commonly used in patients with a history of COPD, are implicated in QT prolongation. In addition, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia as a result of thiazide therapy may increase the risk of torsades. In this case, even in the absence of hypomagnesaemia, some evidence exists though that magnesium loading increases the probability of termination of torsades.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav is not known to increase QT interval.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect. Doxycycline is not known to cause increased QT interval.

Imipenem
Imipenem is incorrect. Imipenem is not known to increase QT interval.

stem: A 72-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation comes to the Emergency Department with bleeding around his gums and extensive bruising. You understand he has recently begun antifungal therapy for a long-standing skin infection, and antibiotics for a respiratory tract infection. He has had problems sleeping over the past 2 months or so. You check his INR, which is measured at 7.8; he has been stable on 3 mg of warfarin for the past 3 months. Which one of the following medications is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Erythromycin
Erythromycin is a CYP450 enzyme inhibitor, so that warfarin drug concentration and INR may increase. The same effect is seen to a lesser extent with clarithromycin, and less so with azithromycin. Antibiotics may also interfere with warfarin effects by altering gut flora and inhibiting vitamin K absorption, although the effects are often less pronounced than effects on liver enzyme activity.

Griseofulvin
Griseofulvin is incorrect. Griseofulvin is a powerful enzyme inducer, which lessens the effectiveness of drugs metabolised by the liver, including warfarin and the oral contraceptive pill.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is incorrect. Rifampicin is a powerful enzyme inducer such that warfarin concentrations and INR would be expected to fall.

St John’s wort
St John’s wort is incorrect. St John’s Wort is a mild antidepressant which acts as a powerful hepatic enzyme inducer, such that warfarin concentrations and INR would be expected to fall.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a suspected stroke. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes and is poorly compliant with her medication. On examination she has loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of her face and the right hand side of her body. There is also dysphagia, slurred speech and nystagmus. Where is the most likely site of the lesion in this patient?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The clinical features described here are those of lateral medullary syndrome. Lateral medullary syndrome is due to vertebral artery occlusion, PICA occlusion or occlusion of the superior, middle or inferior medullary arteries. This patient’s vascular risk factors should be managed aggressively, including with respect to her diabetes control, and she should be prescribed anti-platelet therapy.

Anterior communicating artery
Anterior communicating artery is incorrect. The anterior communicating artery supplies medial aspects of the frontal and parietal lobes, basal ganglia, anterior fornix and anterior corpus callosum. Lesions at this site are often associated with a sensorimotor deficit on the contralateral side.

Internal carotid artery
Internal carotid artery is incorrect. This is associated with transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) and variable MCA/ACA territory strokes.

Lenticulostriate artery
Lenticulostriate artery is incorrect. The lenticulostriate artery supplies the internal capsule.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with a 3-year history of Parkinson’s disease managed with Ropinirole and a small dose of Levodopa comes to the clinic with deteriorating motor symptoms. In particular she is suffering severe dyskinesia, but does not want to reduce the dose of her Parkinson’s medications for fear of increasing rigidity and tremor. Examination in the clinic reveals mild tremor and well-controlled rigidity. She does however have significant dyskinesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Amantadine
In this case, the patient’s dyskinesia is a consequence of relative excess of dopamine, as a result of her antiparkinsonian medications. However, reducing the level or effect of the dopamine will cause a recrudescence of her parkinsonian symptoms. Amantadine reduces dyskinesia without worsening motor function, as it inhibits NMDA receptors rather than through any anti-dopaminergic actions. This will help to reduce the patient’s dyskinesia without affecting her motor function.

Entacapone
Entacapone is incorrect. It is a catechyl-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor primarily used for the treatment of ‘off’ phenomena: it inhibits the breakdown of L-dopa in the brain and consequently prolongs its action. As the dyskinesia is a function of a relative excess of dopamine caused by the patient’s anti-parkinsonian medication, giving a COMT inhibitor such as entacapone will only worsen her dyskinetic symptoms.

Lorazepam
Lorazepam is incorrect. The only way in which this would the patient’s dyskinesia is through sedation, which will be just as disabling as her dyskinesia.

Reduce Levodopa
Reduce L-dopa is incorrect. Although this will certainly her dyskinesia, it will cause an unacceptable worsening of her parkinsonian motor symptoms, which the patient clearly wishes to avoid. Amantadine is a more suitable option as that would not lead to a worsening of her Parkinson’s motor symptoms.

stem: A 69-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Ward with progressive gait disturbance and fluctuating confusion. His symptoms began about six months ago when he noticed heaviness in his legs on walking to work. Since then, his handwriting has become more untidy. His wife reports that he has become increasingly forgetful at home, although he denies this. Over the last two months, he has become restless at night and has reported seeing unidentified objects moving on the walls and in the room. On examination, his Mini-Mental State Examination score is 24/30. He is symmetrically rigid and slow, with a mild, jerky tremor in the upper limbs. Cranial nerve examination is unremarkable. His gait is shuffling, with mildly impaired postural reflexes. The accumulation of which protein causes the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Alpha-synuclein
The combination of progressive cognitive decline, fluctuating symptoms, visual hallucinations, extrapyramidal signs (rigidity and bradykinesia more prominent than tremor) and sleep pattern disturbance suggests a diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. This is caused by an accumulation of an aggregated form of alphasynuclein into Lewy bodies within vulnerable neurons.

Beta-amyloid
Beta-amyloid plaques are insoluble and their presence is found to be associated with Alzheimer’s disease on autopsy. They are detectable in the brain of patients before diagnosis, with subtle effects on cognition.

Prions
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by abnormal proteins with are called prion proteins. Prions are misfolded proteins which induce abnormal folding of other Chat proteins. They difficult to inactivate, whereby alcohol treatment, autoclaving and gamma irradiation are ineffective at disinfecting contaminated equipment.

Serum amyloid A protein
Vascular dementia is a good differential diagnosis, but overall the clinical picture is more suggestive of DLB.

Tau.

stem: A 73-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease presents to the clinic for review. He is taking a combination of a dopamine agonist, levodopa and a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Whilst his motor symptoms are well controlled, his wife is concerned as he is mildly confused, is awake for many hours during the night and is suffering from visual hallucinations, coupled with delusions that she is trying to poison him. He is quiet and withdrawn when you review him in the clinic. His mini-mental state score is 23. He is able to walk across the examination room and perform some fine motor tasks, although is unable to provide a sample of handwriting. Which of the following is the best intervention with respect to controlling his hallucinations?
explanation:
Quetiapine
Management of hallucinations and agitation in association with Parkinson’s disease is difficult. Given that the cause of motor symptoms in Parkinson’s is a lack of dopamine, any medication that reduces dopamine levels or effects can dramatically worsen motor symptoms. Unfortunately, most antipsychotics, and especially the ‘typical’ antipsychotics, do have anti-dopaminergic effects. This leaves low-dose atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine as the most appropriate intervention.

Benzhexol
Benzhexol is incorrect. It is an anticholinergic agent used to manage extrapyramidal side effects suchAIas Tutor dyskinesia. However, its side effects include disturbed sleep and at higher doses it can cause agitation.

Entacapone
Entacapone is incorrect. It is a catechyl-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor and thereby acts to prevent the breakdown of levodopa in the brain, prolonging its effects. It does not have any role in preventing hallucinations or treating agitation.

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is incorrect. Haloperidol is a D2-receptor antagonist; it reduces the effect of dopamine in the brain. Consequently, it can dramatically worsen the motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, and therefore although an effective treatment for hallucinations and agitation, it would be contraindicated for this patient.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her confusion?
explanation:
Digoxin
Digoxin is associated with disorientation, vomiting, mental confusion, amnesia and depression. It is also associated with a yellow visual field discoloration called xanthopsia. Other cardiovascular drugs which cause sleep disturbance include beta-blockers and statins. Interestingly the PDE-5 inhibitors suchChat as sildenafil when with used in high doses may cause blue visual field discoloration, due to cross-reactivity with retinal PDE-6.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Common adverse effects of amlodipine include ankle swelling, rash and gastrointestinal disturbance.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin is a major cause of gastritis, peptic ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is incorrect. Atorvastatin may cause acute delirium but would not typically cause vomiting; recognised adverse effects of statins include myositis and drug-induced hepatitis.

stem: A 78-year-old alcoholic ex-contractor presents with cough, occasional haemoptysis, fever, night sweats and weight loss for the preceding 3 months. He consumes around 60 units of alcohol a week and has a 25 pack/year history. On examination he is cachexic, tachycardic and dyspnoeic on minimal exertion; auscultation reveals diffuse crepitations bilaterally; and there is moderate, mildly tender, bilateral supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. He has a macrocytic anaemia (Hb 93 g/l, MCV 110 fl), deranged LFTs (ALT 248 U/l, AST 720 U/l, GGT 432 U/l, ALP 140 U/l, albumin 15 g/l) and a raised CRP (158 mg/l). A chest X-ray (CXR) shows multiple cavitating lesions in both lung apices. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Necrotising pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus
Infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
explanation:
Tuberculosis (TB)
This gentleman has cavitating pulmonary TB, probably with lymphatic spread. His age and history of chronic alcohol abuse suggest that his immunity is likely compromised. The history of cough, fever, weight loss, haemoptysis, lymphadenopathy and chest X-ray appearance all suggest a diagnosis of TB. A lung malignancy is a possible alternative, but TB must be suspected and thoroughly investigated in an individual with this history, if only due to the public health implications. Drug-sensitive TB is usually treated with four drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide) for at least 6 months: ethambutol and pyrazinamide are normally prescribed for the first 2 months and isoniazid and rifampicin for the full 6 months. However, this gentleman already has signs of liver damage, presumably alcohol-induced, and is high risk for hepatic toxicity caused by pyrazinamide, isoniazid and rifampicin; a so-called ‘liver-friendly’ regime may be considered, which may include injectable streptomycin and moxifloxacin, among others. Individuals with complex co-morbidities, such as this patient, require specialist management and should be discussed or referred as appropriate.

Necrotising pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus
Necrotising pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Individuals with structural lung damage are at greater risk of pneumonia due to S. aureus, which can cause cavitation and abscess formation, most frequently in the right lower zone. However, infection tends to be aggressive and progresses quickly. The relatively long history and constitutional symptoms seen here suggest another process.

Infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is incorrect. Despite his smoking history, the constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy and anaemia suggest there may be another process at work.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is incorrect. SCLC can present with cavitatory lesions on CXR and is closely linked to smoking – this gentleman is certainly at risk. Tumours originate from the bronchial mucosa and as such, over 90% of SCLCs occur centrally, in a lobar or main bronchus. The lymphadenopathy, weight loss and haemoptysis could all be symptomatic of a lung malignancy; SCLC is also associated with various paraneoplastic syndromes, which could cause fever and night sweats, among other symptoms. The likelihood of immune suppression, due to alcohol, and the position of the cavitating lesions make TB the more likely diagnosis; urgent investigation for TB is needed in any case, due to the public health implications of infection.

Pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
Pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. S. pneumoniae is a common cause of communityacquired pneumonia and one would expect to see routine consolidative changes on CXR. The long history and constitutional symptoms present here also make this a less likely primary diagnosis, although many patients with immune suppression and tuberculosis may also have superadded bacterial pneumonia. Further reading NICE. Tuberculosis: Prevention, diagnosis, management and service organisation. NICE guideline 33 (NG33). London: NICE, 2016. ( Gadowski L B, Stout J E. 2008. Cavitary pulmonary disease. Clinical Microbiology Reviews, 21, 2, 305–333.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is referred to the cardiology outpatients department with a history of dizzy episodes and one episode of syncope. She is known to have longstanding paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. A 24-hour tape confirms high burden atrial fibrillation, with rates varying from 30 bpm to 140 bpm. There are several SA block episodes with pauses of > 3 seconds. Sinus node disease appears to be the most likely diagnosis. She is listed for a permanent pacemaker. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate device?
explanation:
DDDR
This woman has atrial fibrillation and, significant pauses/periods of complete heart block. As such, a dual chamber dual sensing rate modulating pacemaker is the best option of all.

DDI
This woman has atrial fibrillation with significant pauses, so it is likely that the natural pacemaker (the sinoatrial node) is unreliable – sinus node disease or sick sinus syndrome. In these cases, a DDI pacemaker could be used, although a dual sensing modulating pacemaker is the best option of all.

VOO
VOO paces at a fixed output setting, simply pacing the ventricle at a fixed rate with no sensing of the ventricle. The pacing may fall in the relative refractory period of the ventricle. This scenario can induce the ‘R-on-T’ phenomenon, which can lead to ventricular tachyarrhythmia and ventricular fibrillation.

VVI
VVI means there is one lead in the ventricle (pacing and sensing the ventricle, indicated by the ‘VV’). If the pacemaker senses an intrinsic QRS complex, then pacing is inhibited (I). This means the pacemaker will deliver a stimulus only if there is a significant pause. VVI pacing in the context of AF is only really considered when there is considerable slowing of the ventricular response, (making up around 10–15% only of indications for pacing).

VDD
VDD is incorrect. Sensing of the atrium is not required because the woman is in atrial fibrillation. Types of pacemakers Pacemaker types are defined by an international code, which uses three or more letters in a set sequence. The first letter is related to the chamber that is to be paced: A = atrium, V = ventricle, D = both The second letter refers to the chamber that is sensed (A, V or D) The third letter refers to the response to a sensed beat by the pacemaker: I = inhibits, T = trigger or D = both (i.e. inhibits or triggers) VOO is a fixed output setting (e.g. pacing at 60 bpm irrespective of intrinsic activity); the ‘O’ as second and third symbol implies that the chamber is not sensed and, therefore, there is no response to a sensed beat The fourth letter refers to whether or not the pacemaker has rate-adaptive properties (R) More information can be found at: www.escardio.org/Guidelines/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/Cardiac-Pacing-and-Cardiac-ResynchronizationTherapy.

stem: An elderly man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedic ambulance after a collapse. He is known to have ischaemic heart disease. Peripheral pulses are absent and ECG reveals wide-complex tachycardia. He has apparently been conversant with the ambulance staff, but is now becoming unresponsive. You manage to elicit a carotid pulse, which seems to be around 200 bpm, and the electronic BP machine measures his BP as 70/40 mmHg. Immediate management consists of which one of the following?
options: A bolus dose of intravenous lidocaine
Intravenous phenylephrine and carotid sinus pressure
explanation:
DC cardioversion
The patient has ventricular tachycardia and is haemodynamically unstable; his blood pressure is low and is causing a loss of consciousness. The most appropriate treatment is an urgent DC cardioversion. Management of VT: Immediate treatment consists of cardioversion followed by a suitable anti-arrhythmic such as amiodarone infusion first line, or if persistent VT despite amiodarone then an infusion of lignocaine (lidocaine). The trigger of VT must be identified and treated immediately – including electrolyte imbalance or cardiac ischaemia. Most of these patients should undergo coronary angiography to exclude an ischaemia causing stenosis. Myocardial infarction (MI) may be the cause of the ventricular tachycardia, hence treatment for MI would be indicated if,after treatment of the VT, there are clear signs to support the need of primary PCI (preferred) or thrombolysis (if PPCI unavailable or time delays make it futile). Programmed stimulation may only be carried out when the patient is stable and is performed invasively in the electrophysiology suite.

Programmed stimulation
Programmed stimulation is incorrect. This is a diagnostic technique used during invasive electrophysiological studies to determine the source of VT before delivering invasive therapies. This cannot be correct during an emergency situation.

Thrombolysis with TPA or streptokinase
Thrombolysis with TPA or streptokinase is incorrect. This may be appropriate if there was evidence of a myocardial infarction triggering the VT. However, the VT must be treated rapidly first before it degenerates into VF and the patient dies.

A bolus dose of intravenous lidocaine
A bolus dose of intravenous lidocaine is incorrect. Lidocaine is used for haemodynamically stable VT – but it is second line, and should be used after amiodarone in the form of an infusion.

Intravenous phenylephrine and carotid sinus pressure
Intravenous phenylephrine and carotid sinus pressure is incorrect. There are data to suggest that a combination of IV phenylephrine (which triggers a reflex increase in cardiac vagal tone) and carotid sinus massage (another driver of increased vagal tone) can terminate VT in some people. However, this would not be the first line treatment in a patient in haemodynamic compromise. Ventricular Tachycardia –.

stem: You suspect carcinoid syndrome. Which of the following symptoms is most likely to be associated with carcinoid in this situation?
explanation:
Facial flushing
Both diarrhoea (80%) and flushing are common in association with carcinoid syndrome, but episodes of flushing are slightly more commonly seen, (in 85% or more of patients). Episodes of flushing may last for anything from 2–5 min to several hours and are related to serotonin- and kallikrein-driven vasodilatation.

Headache
Headache is incorrect. Headache is more commonly seen as a feature of adrenal tumours rather than carcinoid syndrome.

Right sided valvular disease
Right sided cardiac valvular disease is incorrect. Right sided cardiac valvular disease is seen in around 40% of patients with carcinoid syndrome.

Breathlessness
Incorrect. Wheeze and breathlessness can be reported (histamine / bradykinin release) but is not as common as flushing.

Dermatitis
Dermatitis is incorrect. Excessive serotonin can cause depletion in typtophan and subsequent niacin deficiency – ‘Pellagra’; which is associated with dermatitis / dementia and diarrhoea. Unusual and less common than flushing associated with carcinoid.

stem: An elderly, normotensive man with known severe left ventricular dysfunction presents with a regular broadcomplex tachycardia. His blood pressure is stable at 125/70 mmHg; his pulse is 145 bpm. A previous ECG in his records shows that he was in left bundle-branch block 2 years earlier. He is alert and able to respond to questions. Which one of the following drugs would be the first choice in treatment of his underlying rhythm?
explanation:
Amiodarone
A regular, broad complex tachycardia in a patient with structural heart disease is likely to be ventricular tachycardia and should be treated as such until proven otherwise. In this specific case, a sinus ECG with LBBB and a rate of ~150 bpm may point to an SVT with aberrant conduction; however, further information would be needed to safely diagnose this and manage the case differently. Therefore, the correct answer will always require the patient to be managed as VT. As the patient does not have any adverse features, the first line therapy is IV amiodarone (as recommended by the Resuscitation Council (UK) Adult Tachycardiac (with pulse) algorithm). Amiodarone should be administered via a central venous catheter. Avoid using peripheral cannulae as the risk of tissue damage if there is extravasation is high. If the rhythm was an SVT with aberrant conduction, this is also an appropriate treatment.

Sotalol
Sotalol is incorrect. In the context of poor left ventricular function sotalol may provoke circulatory collapse.

Verapamil
Verapamil is incorrect. In the context of poor left ventricular function verapamil in particular may provoke circulatory collapse.

Lidocaine
Lidocaine is incorrect. In the context of poor left ventricular function lidocaine may provoke circulatory collapse.

Flecainide
Flecainide is incorrect. Flecainide, as with all anti-arrhythmics, can have a pro-arrhythmic effect; in this circumstance it may precipitate ventricular fibrillation. The use of flecainide in patients with prior myocardial infarction was shown to significantly increase mortality in the CAST randomised controlled trial. As such, flecainide should be avoided in those patients with known ischaemic heart disease. Ventricular Tachycardia –.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. She was recently discharged from the hospital after being treated for a urinary tract infection. On examination, she is febrile (38.5°C), has crackles in her right lower lung field, and her oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. What is the most likely causative organism for her condition?
explanation:
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MSRA) is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, especially in patients who have been recently hospitalized or have had recent antibiotic exposure. The presence of MRSA in nosocomial infections has increased due to its resistance to multiple antibiotics and its ability to colonise patients during their hospital stay. The symptoms described here, fever, productive cough, and hypoxia, are typical of bacterial pneumonia caused by this pathogen.

Escherichia coli
While E. coli can cause hospital-acquired infections such as urinary tract infections or sepsis, E. coli-related respiratory infections are rare compared to other pathogens like MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Although K. pneumoniae can cause severe pneumonias including those acquired in hospitals (often referred to as 'currant jelly' sputum due to its appearance), it tends not to be the most likely causative organism following recent hospitalisation without more specific risk factors such as alcoholism or diabetes mellitus.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is known for causing severe nosocomial pneumonias but typically affects patients with structural lung disease like cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis rather than those without these conditions. It’s also more common among patients who have been ventilated.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
S. pneumoniae commonly causes community-acquired rather than hospital-acquired pneumonias and would be less expected given this patient’s recent discharge from a healthcare facility where more resistant organisms are prevalent. Hospital-acquired.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic for review. He has had significant problems with choreiform movements over the past few weeks. He has also had difficulty with co-ordination. This is particularly distressing for him in his job as a car mechanic, and he has become unusually low in mood. Where is the likely anatomical lesion?
explanation:
Caudate nucleus
Lesions affecting the caudate nucleus from infarction, in chorea-acanthocytosis syndrome and Huntington’s, are recognised as leading to symptoms of chorea. With the low mood, poor co-ordination and chorea, this man has Huntington’s disease.

Red nucleus
The red nucleus is a structure in the rostral midbrain involved in motor co-ordination of the upper limbs. A lesion in this area would cause problems with arm swing and motor co-ordination of the upper limbs, not chorea.

Hippocampus
The main role of the hippocampus is in memory and spatial navigation. Lesions at this site are linked to Alzheimer’s disease, temporal lobe epilepsy and schizophrenia. This gentleman does not display signs and symptoms associated with these conditions.

Thalamus
The thalamus has a number of functions, acting as a relay between subcortical areas and the cerebral cortex, regulating sleep and wakefulness, and saccade and anti-saccade eye movements. This does not fit with our patient’s symptoms.

Substantia nigra
Lesions affecting the substantia nigra are more likely to lead to symptoms of parkinsonism rather than chorea. Huntington’s.

stem: An 80-year-old nursing home resident with a long-term urinary catheter presents to the Emergency Department with fevers, rigors and suprapubic pain. Urinalysis is positive for nitrites, white cells, blood and protein. He has had a 7-day course of oral co-amoxiclav from his GP for a suspected urinary infection, which he completed 4 days ago. Which one of the following is the most likely reason for treatment failure?
explanation:
Biofilm formation
This patient was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection 10 days before presentation and treated with an appropriate course of antibiotics. There is no note in the case however that the catheter was changed. Bacteria are able to form biofilm over a wide variety of surfaces, particularly prosthetic material, and this can lead to failure of antibiotic therapy. Source control is extremely important in any infection to allow antibiotics to have maximal impact, and this patient’s catheter should consequently have been changed when the infection was initially diagnosed.

Drug interaction
Drug interaction is incorrect. It is important to check for drug interactions – particularly in an elderly patient in whom there may be significant polypharmacy – but the choice of antibiotic here is unlikely to have interacted significantly with other medications to the extent that treatment failure resulted.

Inappropriate antibiotic choice
Inappropriate antibiotic choice is incorrect. Antibiotic guidelines will vary in different areas depending on local resistance patterns; however, in most guidelines co-amoxiclav would be a reasonable choice for with a urinary tract Chat infection in a male patient.

Infection with a multiresistant organism
Infection with a multiresistant organism is incorrect. Had the catheter been changed, then this would probably have been the best answer. Multidrug resistance is an increasing problem, with ESBL (extended spectrum betalactamase)-producing strains particularly relevant in urinary tract infections.

Non-compliance with medication
Non-compliance with medication is incorrect. This patient is in a nursing home, and therefore is likely to be receiving at least some degree of help with his medications, making non-compliance less likely. Urinary Tract Infection –.

stem: Which of the following is most closely linked to a poor post-stroke prognosis?
explanation:
BI 40
BI is a measure of physical functioning and ability to perform activities of daily living (ADL). It is scored from 0 to 100. For ease of analysis, researchers divide the BI score into bands: BI = 80–100 (independent ADL) BI = 50–79 (moderate reduced ADL) BI = 25–49 (low ADL) BI = 0–24 (very low ADL). A score of 40 therefore describes significant impairment of ADLs consistent with a left-sided weakness. Patients with a score of 25–49 are around 60% more likely to die than those with a normal BI score.

Age 74
Age is a poor predictor of prognosis after a stroke as it is no indicator of potential comorbidities that can impact on outcomes. Age is also poorly predictive of stroke severity.

Creatinine 143 µmol/l
A creatinine of 143 µmol/l does indicate renal impairment, which is a predictor of future cardiovascular events, including stroke. It is, however, a weaker prognostic indicator in comparison to the BI. This is because a low BI implies additional susceptibility to respiratory tract infection related to immobility, and possible aspiration and increased risk of falls.

Diastolic BP 95 mmHg
Although her diastolic blood pressure is mildly elevated, it is not closely related to outcomes so soon after the initial stroke. With gradual intensification of blood pressure-lowering medication, it is likely that target BP will be achieved.

Systolic BP 155 mmHg.

stem: A 75-year-old man is admitted from his residential home with right lower lobe pneumonia confirmed on chest X-ray. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2 °C, hypotensive at 80/60 mmHg, with a heart rate of 120/min. O 2 saturation is 90% on 60% FiO 2. You confirm lower zone consolidation on auscultation. Which of the following measurements would be most useful in predicting the severity of this patient's pneumonia?
explanation:
Urea
Of the options listed, only urea is a component of the CURB-65 scoring system used to determine prognosis in pneumonia. The risk of death at 30 days increases as the score increases: • 0 – 0.7% • 1 – 3.2% • 2 – 13.0% • 3 – 17.0% • 4 – 41.5% • 5 – 57.0%.

CRP
CRP is incorrect. CRP is not a component of the CURB-65 scoring system.

Heart rate
Heart rate is incorrect. Heart rate is not a component of the CURB-65 scoring system.

PaCO2
PaCO 2 is incorrect. PaCO 2 is not a component of the CURB-65 scoring system.

PaO2.

stem: An 81-year-old male patient attends the cardiology clinic for his symptoms of fatigue and ankle oedema. Twodimensional echocardiography shows significant ventricular wall thickening and marked dilatation of both atria. The left ventricular myocardium has a granular sparkling appearance. He is referred for holter monitoring and told he will have predominantly symptomatic treatment. Which one of the following conditions is he most likely to have?
explanation:
Amyloid heart disease
This gentleman has cardiac amyloid, characterised by heart failure with a restrictive filling pattern (demonstrated by the enlarged atria). The ventricles are often thick and appear hypertrophied, but in fact have poor systolic and diastolic function. The speckled appearance is very characteristic of amyloid but cannot be used alone to diagnose it. You reach the conclusion that this is amyloid because the echo findings are not consistent with the other answers. The echocardiographic appearances do help exclude the other conditions. In the scenario a Holter test has been ordered. This could point to amyloid, in which bradycardia with 2:1 or complete heart block is common. However, equally, HCMs also have episodes of VT, which Holter monitoring is appropriate to diagnose.

Constrictive pericarditis
Constrictive pericarditis is incorrect. Constrictive pericaridits typically has apparently normal left systolic ventricular function but diastolic filling can be impaired; the ventricular filling is dependent on each other and there is often septal bounce seen on echo; the septum appears to bounce into the LV as the RV fills.

Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Dilated cardiomyopathy will have globally enlarged ventricular dimensions with impaired ventricular contraction.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) has asymmetrical left ventricular hypertrophy. This particularly involves the septum causing outflow tract obstruction. Other findings in HCM include systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflets (‘SAM’).

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Ischaemic cardiomyopathy results from long-term untreated ischaemia and has dilated ventricles with poor function and often regional wall motion abnormalities: the ischaemic areas contract more slowly and less well than the others. There may also be scarred and thin segments where infarction has occurred previously. Amyloidosis A 72-year-old woman, who lives in a residential home because of limited mobility, is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe headache and left sided weakness. Past history of note includes COPD, hypertension and peripheral vascular disease. Apparently other residents in the same home have been affected by food poisoning symptoms, as have children from a nursery, one of who is in the hospital with acute renal impairment. On examination her BP is 155/90 mmHg; pulse is 80/min and regular. Her temperature is 37.9°C. Heart sounds are normal and there is quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest. You notice a purpuric rash affecting both forearms, and petechiae over her upper chest. She has weakness of the left side of her face and her left arm and is moaning because of her headache. Investigations.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with severe back pain. An X-ray shows the presence of osteolytic lesions in his vertebrae and pelvis. He also complains of malaise. There are no other symptoms of note, he takes medication for hypertension but nil else. Blood tests reveal a corrected calcium of 2.78 mmol/L. Which of the following investigations is likely to reveal the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis
The likely diagnosis is multiple myeloma. Immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis is likely to show a paraprotein, usually IgG or IgA. Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm that produces diffuse bone marrow infiltration with a tendency to form localised osteolytic deposits.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is incorrect. An isolated elevated ALP is found in Paget’s disease. Paget’s disease of bone causes localised bone growth and deformity. This is common in the skull and long bones. This may appear on x-ray as both osteolysis and new bone formation.

BCR-ABL gene testing
BCR-ABL gene testing is incorrect. The BCR-ABL gene mutation is found in Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), which is characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells and massive splenomegaly. Osteolytic lesions are not usually seen.

Prostate specific antigen (PSA)
Prostate specific antigen (PSA) is incorrect. The PSA is likely to be elevated in prostatic carcinoma. Prostatic carcinoma is usually accompanied by symptoms of prostatism (hesitancy, frequency, dribbling) and presents with either sclerotic or lytic lesions. The raised calcium level also points towards myeloma here.

Serum calcium
Serum calcium is incorrect. His patient is likely to be hypercalcaemic, due to the osteolytic lesions, but the serum calcium is not diagnostic. Multiple Myeloma A 69-year-old obese woman with a history of type II diabetes is admitted to the Emergency Department with painful erythematous areas affecting a significant portion of skin on both of her inner thighs. On examination, she is pyrexial (39.5°C), her BP is 110/65 mmHg and her pulse 90 bpm. There are extensive areas of bullous impetigo affecting both inner thighs. Wound swabs are taken to establish the causative organism. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following is the most important intervention?
explanation:
Intravenous (IV) 0.9% saline
This patient almost certainly has norovirus with diarrhoea of sudden onset which has spread very rapidly throughout the residential home. Given he has chronic renal impairment and is significantly dehydrated, IV fluid replacement is the most appropriate next step. His symptoms are likely to resolve spontaneously over the course of 24 hours, and he will remain infective for up to 48 hours after the last bout of diarrhoea. Strict hygiene procedures by staff at the home and isolation of residents are crucial to limit the spread.

IV ondansetron
Although IV antiemetics may be useful to shorten the amount of time before which the patient can begin taking oral fluids again, they are not the most important intervention here. The most pressing need is resolution of likely pre-renal failure with IV fluid replacement.

Oral loperamide
Loperamide, a partial opiate agonist used for treatment of diarrhoea, is not recommended for the treatment of infective gastroenteritis. In this situation, loperamide may cause significant abdominal pain and may actually slow clearance of the virus and resolution of symptoms.

Oral ofloxacin
Quinolones were formerly an option for the treatment of infective diarrhoea related to salmonella or campylobacter, particularly in patients with severe comorbidities and/or marked symptoms of dehydration. Quinolones are now rarely used because of risks associated with their use in terms of musculoskeletal and neurological adverse events. They have no role in the treatment of viral gastroenteritis.

Oral rehydration
Oral rehydration is appropriate once this patient’s vomiting has subsided. Currently, with significant active vomiting, there is little role for oral rehydration. IV fluid replacement is the most important next step. Nausea and VomitingA 72-year-old woman with a long history of osteoarthritis, for which she has used codeine-based analgesics, presents to the clinic complaining of diarrhoea. You ask her to keep a stool chart, but during the period of record keeping if anything she tends to report constipation. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
The age of the patient and symptoms described here of jaw claudication and temporal headaches raise the suspicion of temporal arteritis, or giant cell arteritis (GCA), which is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica. It is important to diagnose or exclude GCA quickly, as delayed treatment can lead to permanent loss of eyesight, most commonly from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Initial treatment would be a trial of high-dose corticosteroids. ESR and CRP are typically elevated in GCA, with ESR usually exceeding 50 mm/h, and it can reach higher than 100 mm/h.

Autoimmune profile
Autoimmune profile is incorrect. In GCA, the frequency of RhF, ANA and other autoreactive antibodies are no higher than that of age-matched controls.

Creatinine kinase
Creatinine kinase is incorrect. Creatinine kinase level is high in polymyositis or dermatomyositis, but it would not be raised in either GCA or polymyalgia rheumatica.

CT head
CT head is incorrect. CT head may play a role in ruling out intracranial masses or bleeds, both of which would cause headache, but it would not be useful in definitively diagnosing GCA.

Temporal artery biopsy
Temporal artery biopsy is incorrect. Temporal artery biopsy is the next investigation of choice if ESR is elevated, but it may be normal due to the skip-lesion nature of the disease. Also it is imperative not to wait for this before commencing therapy, as serious neurological sequelae including blindness may occur as a result of delaying therapy. There are three main patterns of vascular damage in temporal arteritis. The most common is the classic pattern, characterised by marked intimal thickening and transmural inflammation. A dense inflammatory infiltrate composed of T cells and histiocytes is present. Giant Cell Arteritis A 72-year-old woman who is known to have dementia and symptoms of parkinsonism comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has suffered from severe vomiting and dehydration over the past few days. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg, with pulse 90/min and regular. There is a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. She is confused and drowsy with rigidity and tremor on neurological examination. Investigations.

stem: Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Right brainstem
Brainstem strokes cause contralateral weakness, and affect the ipsilateral sympathetic pathway causing Horner syndrome, the ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve causing tongue weakness on the affected side Chat (leading to Tutor deviation with AI towards the ipsilateral side), and medial longitudinal fasciculus causing nystagmus as part of an ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia. It can also cause body sensory loss on the contralateral side and facial sensory loss on the ipsilateral side. MRI is the investigation of choice to differentiate between a thromboembolic and a haemorrhagic aetiology. Ultimately the prognosis of brainstem stroke is poor, although antiplatelet agents may reduce the frequency of future cardiovascular events where thromboembolic aetiology is suspected. Brainstem strokes can best be understood using the ‘Brainstem Rules of Four’, which is complex (an excellent explanation is provided in the weblink given below).

Left hemisphere
Left hemisphere is incorrect, as cerebral hemisphere strokes cause contralateral weakness and sensory loss, so left hemisphere stroke would cause right-sided motor and sensory deficit.

Left brainstem
Left brainstem is incorrect. Generally speaking, strokes cause contralateral limb weakness unless they arise in the cerebellum, where they cause ipsilateral features. As brainstem stroke would cause contralateral weakness and sensory loss, the left brainstem stroke in this answer would cause right-sided motor and sensory deficit.

Right cerebellum
Right cerebellum is incorrect, as cerebellar strokes would cause ipsilateral weakness, and would also present with other features of ‘DANISH’ (dysdiadokokinesis, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech, hypotonia).

Right hemisphere
Right hemisphere is incorrect. While right hemisphere stroke would cause a left-sided weakness, the unusual features described here of nystagmus and Horner syndrome are not typical features of hemisphere strokes, but rather strokes caused by disruption of the posterior circulation.

stem: You decide to prescribe an anti-emetic. Which of the following is most appropriate?
explanation:
Ondansetron
All of the options apart from ondansetron are D2 receptor antagonists. As such, given that the patient has symptoms of parkinsonism, use of any of these agents will significantly worsen her motor function. In contrast, ondansetron is a 5HT-3 receptor antagonist which has no impact on motor function in patients dopamineChatwith with related movement disorders. Similar to the use of D2 receptor antagonist drugs for nausea and vomiting in this situation, the use of antipsychotics that act via the same dopamine antagonist pathway also significantly worsens patients’ mobility.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to the Medical Short Stay Unit with a right lower lobe pneumonia. He has multiple medical problems including type 2 diabetes, peripheral arterial disease and moderate renal impairment with a recent creatinine clearance of 30 ml/min. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.2°C, pulse 90/min and regular, and BP 132/82 mmHg. There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation. He has bilateral pitting oedema of both legs and you cannot feel any peripheral pulses below the knees. Which of the following is the most appropriate DVT prophylaxis?
explanation:
Reduced-dose enoxaparin
This choice is appropriate because guidelines suggest that low-molecular-weight heparin can be used at a reduced dose in patients with moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance between 15-30 ml/min). Reduced-dose enoxaparin provides effective anticoagulation while minimising the risk of drug accumulation and subsequent bleeding. Given the patient's medical history, including type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease, reduced-dose enoxaparin offers a balanced approach to preventing DVT without imposing significant additional risks.

Aspirin
While aspirin has antiplatelet properties, it is not effective in preventing venous thromboembolism (VTE) because it does not provide adequate anticoagulation. Aspirin primarily prevents arterial thrombotic events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke, rather than venous clots. In this patient with multiple risk factors for DVT, relying on aspirin would not offer sufficient protection against the formation of venous clots.

Full-dose enoxaparin
Enoxaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin, is primarily eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with renal impairment, especially those with a creatinine clearance of less than 30 ml/min, full-dose enoxaparin can accumulate in the body, increasing the risk of bleeding complications. Therefore, administering a full dose in this patient with moderate renal impairment could lead to serious adverse effects, making it an unsuitable option.

TEDD stockings
TEDD stockings may worsen peripheral arterial disease by further compromising blood flow in patients with already impaired circulation. In addition, stockings are not as effective as pharmacological agents like lowmolecular-weight heparin for DVT prophylaxis, especially in high-risk patients. Given this patient's background of peripheral arterial disease, using TEDD stockings could potentially exacerbate his condition and provide insufficient prophylaxis.

Unfractionated heparin.

stem: A 78-year-old man attends for review; his relatives are concerned that he is becoming mentally ‘slow’ and rather forgetful. Which one of the following features would be most suggestive of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)?
explanation:
Detailed visual hallucinations
Formal diagnostic criteria for DLB make reference to three ‘core’ clinical features: Features of parkinsonism Well-formed and detailed visual hallucinations Fluctuating cognition with variations in attention and alertness. There are a number of other features that might prompt consideration of the diagnosis (referred to as ‘suggestive’ and ‘supportive’ features) Repeated falls Syncope or transient loss of consciousness Severe autonomic dysfunction (urinary incontinence, orthostatic hypotension) Neuroleptic hypersensitivity.

Disinhibition
Disinhibition is incorrect. This is not a feature of DLB and would be more in keeping with a diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia.

Emotional lability
Emotional lability is incorrect. Emotional disturbance can be seen in various types of dementia but a labile mood (particularly with sudden explosive outbursts of crying and laughing) is perhaps most oftenChat seenwith in vascular dementia.

Good response to dopaminergic therapy
Good response to dopaminergic therapy is incorrect. Unfortunately, the use of dopaminergic therapy for motor symptoms often leads to a worsening of visual hallucinations in DLB.

Paucity of extrapyramidal signs
Paucity of extrapyramidal signs is incorrect. The presence of parkinsonism is a core clinical feature of DLB.

stem: A 73-year-old woman who has recently started anti-tuberculous therapy is referred to the anti-coagulation clinic, as despite recent increases in her warfarin dose, the INR had continued to fall progressively from 2.5 to 1.3. Which of the following medications is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Rifampicin
Rifampicin is a potent CYP450 enzyme inducer; as such it is likely to be responsible for increasing the extent of warfarin metabolism and consequent fall in INR.

Ethambutol
Ethambutol is incorrect. Ethambutol is primarily an inhibitor of CYP1A2 and 2E1 and has lesser inhibitory effects on 2A6, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6 and 3A4; as such it may increase the INR rather than decrease it.

Isoniazid
Isoniazid is incorrect. Isoniazid is an inhibitor of 2C19 and 3A4, as warfarin is metabolised by the 2C9 isoenzyme isoniazid is unlikely to alter INR.

Pyrazinamide
Pyrazinamide is incorrect. Pyrazinamide does not have significant drug interactions mediated by the p450 system.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of slurred speech and trouble swallowing, with dizziness. On examination there is bilateral nystagmus, and he has loss of pinprick sensation over his left arm and leg, and the right hand side of his face. Which of these arteries is most likely to be involved?
explanation:
Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
This patient has lateral medullary syndrome, caused by infarction of the lateral portion of the medulla oblongata. The area is supplied by either the posterior inferior cerebellar artery or the vertebral artery (not offered as an option here). The neurological features seen here are typical of the condition: loss of pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral side of the body and the ipsilateral side of the face; dysphagia; dysarthria; vertigo; and nystagmus. Management involves anti-platelet therapy and a work-up to rule out cardiac emboli (i.e. echocardiography and Holter ECG monitor), which may require long-term anti-coagulation.

Left posterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery is incorrect. A posterior cerebral artery stroke would lead to visual disturbance (i.e. visual field loss, or higher disturbances such as palinopsia). It would not explain the cerebellar seen here. Chatsigns with Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery is incorrect. An infarct or haemorrhage in this territory would also cause a lateral medullary syndrome. However, the loss of pain and temperature sensation would be on the right side of the body and the left side of the face (the opposite to the signs in this case).

Right anterior cerebral artery
Right anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. An anterior cerebral artery stroke would cause contralateral hemiparesis, with weakness more pronounced in the leg than in the arm. This patient does not have any weakness. If this was an anterior cerebral artery stroke, you would not expect to see the cerebellar and posterior territory signs that this patient displays.

Right posterior cerebral artery
Right posterior cerebral artery is incorrect. A posterior cerebral artery stroke would not cause cerebellar symptoms. This patient does not complain of any visual disturbance (e.g. field loss, or higher visual disturbances such as palinopsia), which you would expect to find in a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

stem: A 72-year-old man with known metastases as a result of disseminated prostate cancer comes to the Emergency Department for review with increased tiredness. Despite hormonal therapy, his PSA has risen slowly over the past few months, and he has required a blood transfusion some 3 months ago. On examination, his BP is 105/70 mmHg; pulse is 95/min and regular. He looks pale and is complaining of pain in his lower back and right femur. A bone scan report from some 4 months ago reveals extensive bony metastases. The Hb on the blood gas machine is 81 g/l. Which of the following is the most likely finding on the standard blood film?
explanation:
Nucleated red cells
Nucleated red cells are the most likely finding on the blood film. This man has metastatic prostatic carcinoma with bony metastasis. He is anaemic. Therefore a leucoerythroblastic blood picture is most likely. This essentially will demonstrate early red and white blood cell precursors in the peripheral blood film. The early red blood cell precursors will be nucleated red blood cells; the early white blood cell precursors will include promyelocytes, myelocytes and band cells, which are normally found in the bone marrow, and not in the peripheral blood.

Heinz bodies
Heinz bodies is incorrect. Heinz bodies are seen in haemolytic anaemia and consist of denatured haemoglobin.

Howell-Jolly bodies
Howell–Jolly bodies is incorrect. Howell–Jolly bodies are seen in patients with hyposplenism.

Low/absent reticulocytes
Low/absent reticulocytes is incorrect. Reticulocytes can only be seen on the blood film with special stains.

stem: The blood smear shows hypochromic, microcytic erythrocytes. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Iron deficiency anaemia
This lady has a microcytic anaemia associated with a thrombocytosis. The anaemia is quite significant, and the microcytosis is quite pronounced, suggesting iron deficiency anaemia more than the anaemia of chronic disease.

Anaemia of chronic disease
Anaemia of chronic disease is incorrect. This is a significant anaemia with a significant microcytosis. In the anaemia of chronic disease, it is rare for the haemoglobin to be less than 8 gm/dl, and one would not expect such a significant microcytosis.

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia rarely causes microcytosis.

Folate deficiency anaemia
Folate deficiency anaemia is incorrect. Folate deficiency anaemia would be expected to cause a macrocytosis not a microcytosis.

Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.

stem: Smudge cells seen on peripheral blood smear. Which one of the following represents the most appropriate therapy for this patient?
explanation:
Chlorambucil
Single agent chlorambucil would be an appropriate treatment for this elderly lady who appears to have chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). She has symptomatic disease in that she is losing weight, and she is also anaemic. Single agent chlorambucil is well tolerated in this age group, and does not usually cause significant cytopaenias.

Busulfan
Busulfan is incorrect. Busulfan is used sometimes in myeloproliferative conditions, but usually not in CLL.

Fludarabine
Fludarabine is incorrect. Fludarabine does have activity against CLL. This is seldom used any longer as a single agent. In addition, caution has to be used in elderly patients, and those with renal impairment, and we can see that the creatinine here is borderline at 120.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Again, prednisolone can have some activity against CLL, but single agent cytotoxic therapy with chlorambucil is usually preferred.

stem: A 62-year-old woman who was treated by a locum GP after a urinary tract infection asks to see the emergency doctor after feeling something 'go' in her ankle and then complaining of an inability to walk on tip toe. She is concerned that it may be related to her antibiotic therapy. On examination, she appears to have a partial rupture of her right Achille's tendon. Which one of the following antibiotics is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Ciprofloxacin
Tendon rupture as a consequence of antibiotic therapy An association between quinolones and tendon rupture exists, although the evidence for causation is poor, and the possible mechanism is uncertain. A number of case control studies suggest an association between quinolone use and tendon rupture, particularly in an elderly population and where concomitant steroid use has occurred. These studies demonstrate that the risk of rupture may be up to seven-fold higher than that in untreated individuals.

Clarithromycin
Clarithromycin is incorrect. Clarithromycin is not known to increase the risk of tendon rupture. Typical adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and rash, and macrolides are subject to multiple drug interactions through their inhibitory effects on hepatic enzyme activity.

Erythromycin
Erythromycin is incorrect. Erythromycin is not known to increase the risk of tendon rupture. Typical adverse with effects include gastrointestinal upset and rash, and macrolides are subject to multiple drug Chat interactions through their inhibitory effects on hepatic enzyme activity.

Gentamicin
Gentamicin is incorrect. Gentamicin is not known to increase the risk of tendon rupture. Typical adverse effects include acute kidney injury and ototoxicity.

Penicillin
Penicillin is incorrect. Penicillin is not known to increase the risk of tendon rupture. Typical adverse effects include rash, gastrointestinal symptoms and allergy.

stem: A 71-year-old man has come to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He lost his hair in his early thirties, and is concerned about sun exposure from living in South Africa for many years. Examination of the scalp reveals a number of erythematous plaque-like lesions; biopsy of two of them reveals proliferation of atypical keratinocytes within the epidermis. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat these lesions?
explanation:
Topical fluorouracil 5% cream (5-FU)
A networked meta-analysis of 26 individual trials for actinic keratosis provides us with the best evidence with respect to managing this condition. The analysis suggests that topical 5-FU is the most effective treatment, followed by: 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy; topical imiquimod; 5-methylaminolaevulinate photodynamic therapy; cryotherapy; topical diclofenac with hyaluronic acid; and placebo. Where there is not significant hyperkeratosis, 5-FU is said to result in clearance of lesions in >90% of cases.

Superficial radiotherapy
Superficial radiotherapy is incorrect. This is a clear diagnosis of multiple actinic keratoses. Radiotherapy can be used in a number of skin cancers (either when primary excision is not feasible or as an adjuvant treatment in order to suppress tumour recurrence), but is not indicated in the treatment of actinic keratoses.

Surgical excision
Surgical excision is incorrect. Surgical excision of multiple lesions on the scalp would lead to significant iatrogenic morbidity. Alternative topical treatments are much better tolerated for such lesions and should be employed instead.

Topical hydrocortisone 1% cream
Topical hydrocortisone 1% cream is incorrect. This product is used to treat inflammatory skin condition such as eczema and psoriasis, but is not used in the management of actinic keratoses.

Narrow-band UVB phototherapy.

stem: A 71-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review of an irregular red area, around 10 mm in diameter, to the left of her nose. She tells you that she thinks that the lesion began as a freckle, and that she has had significant sun damage from many years living in Australia in the past. On examination there is a small lesion to the left of her nose, with evidence of extensive skin damage to her face. Biopsy is described as being consistent with lentigo maligna. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Surgical excision
Surgical excision remains the therapy of choice for lentigo maligna.

Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy is incorrect. Cryotherapy is considered subsidiary to surgery because of a high risk of recurrence, and the possibility that melanoma in situ may be missed if non-surgical therapies are pursued first.

Imiquimod
Imiquimod is incorrect. However, imiquimod cream used post-surgical excision may reduce the risk of recurrence.

Radiotherapy
Radiotherapy is incorrect. Radiotherapy is considered subsidiary to surgery because of a high risk of recurrence, and the possibility that melanoma in situ may be missed if non-surgical therapies are pursued first.

Topical 5-fluorouracil.

stem: A hypertensive, heavy-smoking, 73-year-old man suffers a massive cardiac infarct following occlusion of his anterior interventricular artery (anterior descending artery). Angiography is performed to demonstrate the coronary vessels. Which anatomical relationship of these vessels should be borne in mind?
options: The circumflex artery is the major branch of the right coronary artery
The left anterior descending artery arises above the left posterior aortic cusp
The left anterior descending artery supplies the majority of the left ventricle
The posterior interventricular artery is a branch of the circumflex artery
There is a rich collateral circulation between the right and left coronary arteries
explanation:
The left anterior descending artery supplies the majority of the left ventricle
Occlusion of the artery drives presentation with an extensive anterior myocardial infarction.

The circumflex artery is the major branch of the right coronary artery
The circumflex artery is the major branch of the right coronary artery is incorrect. The circumflex is a branch of the left coronary artery and supplies the posterolateral left ventricle and the anterolateral papillary muscle. It also supplies the sinoatrial nodal artery in 38% of people. The artery supplies 15–25% of the left ventricle in right-dominant systems. If the coronary anatomy is left-dominant, it supplies 40–50% of the left ventricle.

The left anterior descending artery arises above the left posterior aortic cusp
The left anterior descending artery arises above the left posterior aortic cusp is incorrect. It is the left coronary artery that arises above the left aortic cusp. This divides to form the circumflex and left anterior descending arteries.

The posterior interventricular artery is a branch of the circumflex artery
The posterior interventricular artery is a branch of the circumflex artery is incorrect. This arises from the right coronary artery and supplies the posterior one-third of the interventricular septum.

There is a rich collateral circulation between the right and left coronary arteries.

stem: An elderly man with a right iliofemoral DVT is treated with heparin, but later returns with a painful, white, ischaemic foot. Investigations initially show: Hb normal, Plt 20, WCC normal, APTT 24.6. On day 7,Hb dropped from 16 to 14 with reduced platelet count. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Stop heparin
Stopping heparin is the most appropriate management step. This man presented with a venous thrombotic event and is treated with heparin. He later returns with a painful, white,ischaemic foot. This now suggests he has an arterial thrombosis. This, associated with a thrombocytopaenia, suggests the development of heparininduced thrombocytopaenia. The most important management step is to stop heparin, and then institute an alternative anticoagulant.

Give blood
Give blood is incorrect. Giving blood is not the next most appropriate step. The most important management step is to stop the heparin immediately and institute an alternative anticoagulant.

Hirudin
Hirudin is incorrect. Hirudin is not widely available. The institution of an alternative anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux would be appropriate while undertaking further investigations.

Low-molecular-weight heparin
Low-molecular-weight heparin is incorrect. There is cross-reactivity with unfractionated heparin, and indeed low-molecular-weight heparin in its own right can cause heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia. This is not an appropriate alternative to intravenous heparin in this situation.

Platelet transfusion.

stem: A 78-year-old man had poliomyelitis as a child, which left him with total paralysis of the left deltoid muscle. Which feature is most likely to be present on clinical examination?
options: Abduction of the shoulder to 60° is likely to be preserved owing to action of the intact supraspinatus
Anaesthesia over the ‘epaulette’ region of the left shoulder
Detectable weakness in drawing the arm forward and internally rotating the shoulder when this is
Drooping of the left shoulder compared with the right side
The acromion process of the scapula forms the most lateral bony landmark of the left shoulder
explanation:
Detectable weakness in drawing the arm forward and internally rotating the shoulder when this is
Detectable weakness in drawing the arm forward and internally rotating the shoulder when this is compared with the right side Paralysis of the deltoid muscle causes weakness of shoulder abduction, particularly after 30° of abduction. The supraspinatus initiates abduction of the shoulder in the first 30° of movement, therefore this part of the shoulder abduction may be spared (especially in athletes presenting sports injury to the axillary nerve, for example, who may have hypertrophied supraspinati). The deltoid, in addition to being the powerful abductor of the shoulder, assists in flexion and medial rotation (and extension and lateral rotation) of the shoulder by means of its anterior and posterior fibres, respectively. Weakness of these movements compared with the normal side can be detected on careful examination.

Abduction of the shoulder to 60° is likely to be preserved owing to action of the intact supraspinatus
Abduction of the shoulder to 60° is likely to be preserved owing to action of the intact supraspinatus muscle on the left side Abduction of the shoulder to 60° is likely to be preserved owing to action of the intact supraspinatus muscle on the left side is incorrect. Supraspinatus only assists with the first 30° of abduction.

Anaesthesia over the ‘epaulette’ region of the left shoulder Anaesthesia over the ‘epaulette’ region of the left shoulder is incorrect. This area is suppliedChat by awith sensory branch of the axillary nerve. Polio should leave this unaffected.

Drooping of the left shoulder compared with the right side
Drooping of the left shoulder compared with the right side is incorrect. Scapular elevation is via the levator scapulae, and the upper fibres of the trapezius.

The acromion process of the scapula forms the most lateral bony landmark of the left shoulder.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker recently underwent radiotherapy for an inoperable lung carcinoma. He presents to the Emergency Department because his carer noticed significant bruising and bleeding, which she could not stop, after she was shaving him that morning. On examination he is cachectic and jaundiced. The following laboratory results are obtained. Hb, WCC normal and MCV elevated, thrombocytes 33 × 10 9/litre, PT, APTT and bleeding time prolonged, fibrinogen levels decreased. Which one of the following is the most likely cause for this patient’s bleeding tendency?
explanation:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
This man has advanced lung cancer. He has thrombocytopenia, evidence of a prolonged PT, APTT, as well as reduced fibrinogen levels. The fact that he has an advanced malignancy, low platelets and prolonged coagulation times with a low serum fibrinogen all suggests underlying disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to his lung carcinoma.

Liver metastases
Liver metastases is incorrect. Although liver metastases may have some effect on coagulation factor production, this would not really explain the very low platelet count at 33 × 10 9/litre and rapidity that these symptoms have occurred.

Fibrin deficiency
Fibrin deficiency is incorrect because it clearly has nothing to do with the fact that this man has an inoperable lung carcinoma. Primary fibrin deficiency is extremely rare and again would not explain the low platelet count.

Warfarin overdose
Warfarin overdose is incorrect. There is nothing to suggest that this man is on warfarin! It would cause a definite prolongation of the PT, a lesser prolongation of the APTT, but would not normally affect fibrinogen levels or platelet count.

Bone metastases.

stem: An 81-year-old man with a 20-year history of type II diabetes mellitus visits his general practitioner (GP) for a routine check-up. His GP carries out a thorough check for diabetes mellitus and discovers peripheral and autonomic neuropathy. The man comments that at times he feels that he is short of breath upon exertion and that he has some swelling of his ankles. The GP does an electrocardiogram that shows left bundle branch block (LBBB). What is the most likely cause in this case?
explanation:
Ischaemic heart disease
LBBB occurs in ischaemic heart disease. A patient with symptoms suspicious of myocardial infarction and new (or presumed new) LBBB denotes a ST elevation myocardial infarction that requires urgent reperfusion therapy. Other causes of LBBB are: Aortic stenosis Dilated cardiomyopathy Acute myocardial infarction Extensive coronary artery disease Primary disease of the cardiac electrical conduction system Longstanding hypertension leading to dilatation of aortic roots and subsequent aortic regurgitation Lyme disease Side effects of some types of cardiac surgery (eg reconstruction of aortic roots). Diagnostic criteria of LBBB on the electrocardiogram: The heart rhythm must be supraventricular in origin The QRS duration must be ≥ 120 ms There should be a QS or rS complex in lead V1 There should be a notched (‘M’-shaped) R wave in lead V6 The T wave should be deflected opposite the terminal deflection of the QRS complex (‘appropriate T wave discordance with bundle branch block’). A concordant T wave may suggest ischaemia or myocardial infarction. There are partial blocks of the left bundle branch: ‘left anterior fascicular block’ and ‘left posterior fascicular block’. This refers to bifurcation of the left bundle branch.

Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is incorrect. Mitral stenosis is associated with right ventricular strain and hypertrophy with partial or complete right bundle branch block (RBBB). Causes of RBBB: Atrial septal defect Brugada syndrome Right ventricular hypertrophy Pulmonary embolism Ischaemic heart disease Rheumatic heart disease Myocarditis Cardiomyopathy Hypertension.

Pericarditis
Pericarditis is incorrect. Pericarditis is not associated with bundle branch block.

Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is associated with right ventricular strain and hypertrophy with partial or complete right bundle branch block (RBBB).

Tricuspid stenosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man comes to see you with chronic back pain, which worsened one week ago. He has been wheelchair-bound for six months because of severe osteoporosis with multiple lumbosacral spine fractures. He has severe asthma, which has required large doses of glucocorticoids for many years. The patient reports a progressive loss of height and kyphosis over the past year. Other medications include salbutamol and ipratropium inhalers and long-acting theophylline 300 mg twice a day. Significant physical findings include bilateral cataracts, multiple ecchymoses and a prolonged expiratory phase with bilateral wheezes. Calcium and phosphate are in the middle of the normal range. Which of the following treatments would be the first choice in this patient for treatment of his bone disease?
explanation:
Bisphosphonate therapy
This patient has significant osteoporosis, almost certainly related to chronic use of glucocorticoid therapy for his asthma. First-line therapy in this case would be bisphosphonates, which bone mass in the lumbar spine and the hip. Daily preparations were associated with significant gastrointestinal (GI) side-effects (predominantly oesophagitis and ulceration), although weekly and monthly options are now available with less propensity for GI adverse effects. An IV infusion is also a potential delivery option for bisphosphonates.

Testosterone replacement
Tesotsterone replacement is incorrect. In this situation we are given no indication of androgen deficiency. The loss of bone mineral density is most likely due to chronic corticosteroid use. As such testosterone is not of value here.

Vitamin D supplementation
Vitamin D supplementation is incorrect. Vitamin D supplementation is given to treat osteoporosis, but used alone it is very much inferior to other options including bisphosphonates. The calcium and phosphate in the normal range would also not fit well with vitamin D deficiency.

Calcium supplementation
Calcium supplementation is incorrect. Like vitamin D, calcium alone is inadequate as a treatment for osteoporosis.

Calcitonin therapy.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents in an acute confusional state. His plasma sodium concentration is 108 mmol/l; his creatinine is 106 μmol/l and urea 5.0 mmol/l. Which one of the following findings would be most suggestive of the hyponatraemia being caused by inappropriate secretion of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone, ADH)?
explanation:
Spot urine osmolality 510 mosmol/kg
The finding of a urinary osmolality higher than that of plasma implies defective water excretion and is characteristic of inappropriate secretion of ADH.

Plasma albumin concentration of 28 g/l
Plasma albumin concentration of 28 g/l is incorrect as hypoalbuminaema reflects dilution as a result of water overload, irrespective of the cause.

Plasma osmolality of 230 mosmol/kg
Plasma osmolality of 230 mosmol/kg is incorrect. Assuming no great abnormality in glucose level, the plasma osmolality is likely to be low in the general region of 227 mosm/l as in this answer: (2 × Na of 108) + Urea of 5 + Glucose of say 6. This is not the correct answer because low plasma osmolality may be just as likely to be due to fluid overload rather than SIADH.

Plasma urea concentration 2.5 mmol/l
Plasma urea concentration 2.5 mmol/l is incorrect. Low urea reflects dilution due to water overload, regardless of cause.

Urine sodium concentration of 15 mmol/l.

stem: A 76-year-old man has had severe depression with psychotic ideas. He has been an inpatient on a Psychiatric Ward for three months. Despite having received two different antidepressants, both at adequate doses for an adequate period, his mood had continued to deteriorate. He is now refusing to eat, as he says his food is poisoned and is drinking only minimal fluids. He is becoming dehydrated. What would be the next treatment step?
options: Prescription of a third, different antidepressant
explanation:
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
ECT is recommended in the treatment of life-threatening depressive stupor, especially when a patient is refusing to eat and drink. This is used as it generally has a shorter onset of action than antidepressant medication, which takes 2–3 weeks to work. ECT is also recommended as a treatment for treatment-resistant depression, which this man also has.

Prescription of a third, different antidepressant
Prescription of a third, different antidepressant is incorrect. The patient’s symptoms are life threatening and medication has a delay in onset of effect.

Prescription of two antidepressants simultaneously
Prescription of two antidepressants simultaneously is incorrect. Medication has a delay in onset of effect, and combined antidepressants have a risk of drug interactions and should only be prescribed by specialist mental health professionals.

Prescription of an antipsychotic agent
Prescription of an antipsychotic agent is incorrect, this is unlikely to have an effect on his severe depressive symptoms, which are currently life threatening.

Lithium augmentation therapy.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension is admitted to the Emergency Department by the ambulance team. He collapsed, having got up from the lunch table complaining of sudden severe headache and neck pain. On arrival in the Emergency Department he is unconscious with a GCS of 5. His BP is 190/110 mmHg. He is intubated and ventilated and a CT is performed, which reveals a large pontine haemorrhage. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be responsible for the bleed?
explanation:
Basilar
The pons is part of the human brainstem and is supplied by small pontine branches of the basilar artery. These are well-recognised sites of intracerebral haemorrhage related to poorly controlled hypertension and arteriovenous malformations. Large strokes in this region are associated with significant mortality.

Anterior cerebral
